en: The first question:

We shall explain the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). Beforehand, he prepares the necessary materials: a fuel-stick (*idhma*) made of *palāśa*, *khadira*, *udumbara*, or *vaikaṅkata* wood; from that same tree, he makes a ladle (*darvī*) with a hollowed-out bowl, the handle being made of the root-wood, twelve finger-breadths long, and the bowl four finger-breadths deep. It is known from tradition that this constitutes the ritual procedure for the placement of the vessels.

One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception, a Rājanya in the eleventh year from conception, and a Vaiśya in the twelfth year from conception; or, according to another tradition, in the ninth year for a Brāhmaṇa. Regarding garments, they prescribe: a Brāhmaṇa should wear the skin of the Eṇa deer, a Rājanya the skin of the Ruru deer, and a Vaiśya the skin of the goat. It is known from the tradition: "If he wears the skin, he increases spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*); if he wears a garment, he increases royal power (*kṣatra*); both should be worn for the increase of both. One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in spring, or in summer or winter.

In autumn for a Kṣatriya, in the rainy season for a Vaiśya, or in the cool season for a Rathakāra—or indeed for all of them during the waxing fortnight under an auspicious lunar mansion, especially one with a masculine name—he causes the hair of the boy, who has been fed to satiety, to be shaved; having bathed him and adorned him, he causes him to put on a new garment. On a site that slopes toward the east, or toward the north, or on level ground, he raises an altar, sprinkles it with water, churns fire or brings common fire, deposits it, and adds fuel to it. 1.

He strews darbha grass around the fire with the tips pointing eastward; alternatively, the blades may point northward at the rear and front. The southern side is above and the northern side is below. Having strewn darbha grass in the seat of the Brahman priest to the south of the fire with the formula, "I take Agni first within myself," and having meditated upon Agni within himself, he strews grass to the north of the fire for the vessels and arranges the materials as required: a stone, an unwashed garment, a deerskin, and a triple-stranded girdle of muñja grass for a Brāhmaṇa.

He prepares a bowstring for a Kṣatriya and one of *sūtra* grass for a Vaiśya; a staff of *bilva* or *palāśa* wood for a Brāhmaṇa, one of *nyagrodha* wood for a Kṣatriya, and one of *udumbara* wood for a Vaiśya; he binds together a fuel-wood bundle (*idhma*) of twenty-one sticks, or a quantity equal to the number of oblations. Upon it, he fastens the *śamyā*-pins as enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), as well as the wooden spoon (*darvī*), the bunch of grass (*kūrca*), the butter-pot (*ājyasthālī*), the vessel for carrying forward the water (*praṇītāpraṇayana*), the vessel for sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇīpātra*), the fire-brick (*upaveṣa*), and whatever else is required. All these may be bound at once or arranged as they become available; at this time, the Brahman priest puts on his sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).

Having sipped water and stepped past the fire from the west, he throws away a blade of grass from his seat to the south of the *brahmā*-position, touches water, and sits down facing the fire. Having sat down to the west of the fire facing eastward, he prepares two *pavitra* strainers from two *darbha* blades that are equal, with unbroken tips, and a span in length; having cut them with something other than his fingernails and wiped them with water, [he places them on the *kūrca*].

Having poured water into the vessel over which the strainers have been placed, and having filled the vessel so that its rim is level with the water, he purifies it three times by pouring [the water] upwards through the two strainers whose tips point northward. Holding [the vessel] level with his breath and without spilling, he carries it across to the north of the fire. Having set down the *praṇītā* waters, he covers them with *darbha* grass. Having prepared the *prokṣaṇī* waters in the same manner as the *praṇītās*, and having turned the vessels with their openings upward, he places the fuel upon them. He sprinkles all of them three times with the entire quantity of *prokṣaṇī* water. Having heated the ladle (*darvī*) and wiped it clean, and having heated it again, he sets it down.

Having sprinkled the broom with water, he places it into the fire. Having poured the clarified butter into the butter-pot over which the strainers have been laid, having pushed out embers to the north of the fire, having placed [the pot] upon them, having illuminated it, having thrown two young *darbha* blades into it, having carried fire around it three times, having removed it to the north, and having pushed back the embers, he purifies [the butter] three times by moving the strainers back and forth with their tips pointing north. Having placed the two strainers into the fire, he encloses [the hearth] with yoke-pins (*śamyā*). To the west of the fire, he places a yoke-pin with its thick end pointing north, touching the middle one.

To the east of the water-jar, to the south and north, and behind the fire, he places a bundle of grass (kūrca) with its tips pointing north; upon it, having arranged his sacred thread (yajñopavīta), having sipped water, he sits down facing east. The youth, sitting to the south, takes hold of him from behind. 3.

Then he sprinkles water around [the fire]: "O Aditi, give your consent," on the south; "O Anumati, give your consent," on the west; "O Sarasvatī, give your consent," on the north; and "O God Savitṛ, impel [the sacrifice]," all around. Having thus offered the oblations, he sprinkles water around it. Having anointed the fuel-stick (idhma) three times with clarified butter while reciting the formulas used for the prepared offering, he places it on the fire only once, saying: "This fuel is your self, O Jātavedas; grow by it, and cause us to grow. Prosper us with offspring, cattle, Vedic splendor, and the enjoyment of food—svāhā! This is the subsequent [formula].

Having moved the spoon along the junction of the enclosing sticks while seated facing southeast, he pours the *āghāra* libation continuously and straight forward, meditating on Prajāpati in his mind, and does not utter "svāhā. Having moved [the spoon] along the southern junction of the enclosing sticks, he pours the *āghāra* libation continuously and straight forward toward the northeast, saying, "To Indra, svāhā! Then he offers the two *ājyabhāga* portions: in the eastern part of the northern half [of the fire], saying, "To Agni, lord of the sacrifice, svāhā!"; and in the eastern part of the southern half, saying, "To Soma, lord of the sacrifice, svāhā! The other [offerings] are made between these two.

He offers oblations; this is the rule for all *darvihoma* offerings: at the end of a mantra, the utterance *svāhā* is obligatory. In the case of mantras that do not specify a deity, one says "*svāhā* to such-and-such" according to the respective deity; if no deity has been specified, [one offers] to Agni, to Soma, to Prajāpati, to the Viśvedevas, and to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, saying "*svāhā*" for each. He offers with the *vyāhṛtis*, both individually and collectively. 4.

Then he offers these oblations with [the verses]: "You who lie across, saying 'I am the supporter,' you, who belong to Viśvakarman, I sacrifice to you with a stream of ghee—svāhā! You who lie lengthwise, saying 'I am the propitiator,' you, the propitiator, I worship in the fire with a stream of ghee—svāhā! Svāhā to the goddess Saṃrādhinī! Svāhā to the goddess Prasādhinī! I have sought Sadasaspati, the wonderful, the beloved of Indra, the desirable, the winner of wealth, and wisdom—svāhā!"

"Be intent, O Jātavedas Agni; carry [the oblation] forward and know this rite being performed. You are the physician, the maker of the remedy; through you may we obtain cattle, horses, and men—Svāhā! O God, giver of life, being praised for old age, O Agni with a face of ghee and a back of ghee, drinking the ghee and the lovely nectar of the cow, lead this man to old age like a father his son—Svāhā! Then he smooths the ends of the garment, [reciting]: "The goddesses who cut, who spun, who wove, and who bestowed the ends on both sides."

"May these goddesses clothe you for old age; long-lived, put on this garment. Thus he causes him to put it on with [the verse]: "Clothe him, dress him in a garment; make him live for a hundred years, grant him long life. Bṛhaspati gave this garment to King Soma that he might put it on. Go to old age, put on the garment; become a protector against the curses of the people. Live a hundred autumns, full of splendor, and clothe yourself in the increase of wealth. (5)

He addresses the garment that has been put on: "Thou hast put this garment on for well-being; thou hast become a protector against curses among the waters. Live a hundred long autumns, and while living, distribute riches as a noble man. Then he takes his first garment: "May all the gods protect thee, whose first garment we take away."

Or let his brothers and friends follow him as he grows, saying, "Well-born is he! Then he girds him at the waist with a triple-stranded girdle of muñja grass with the verse: "The sister of the gods, this blessed girdle, has come to us—vast, bestowing protection, purifying, and granting refuge; bringing strength through out-breath and in-breath. He ties the knot with the formula: "Thou art the knot of the vital breaths; do not loosen from me. Then he puts on an upper garment of deerskin with the verse: "The eye of Mitra, the supporter, powerful, brilliant, glorious, firm, and kindled."

"An unwashed garment that is worn out, this skin of a conqueror I put on. Having offered these oblations—namely the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *nāṣṭrabhṛt*—he offers these [additional] oblations: "Full behind," "This for me, O Varuṇa," "That I implore of thee," "Thou for us, O Agni," "So thou for us, O Agni," "Thou, O Agni, art the messenger," "And thou, O Agni, art the messenger," "And [grant] freedom from imprecations," "Whatever I have done in excess of this rite," and "O Prajāpati. Having offered the final oblation, he gives a choice gift to his teacher.

To the west of the fire, he spreads two sets of *darbha* grass, one set facing east and the other facing west, with their tips pointing north. Upon these, the two stand facing each other—one facing east and the other facing west—and he should take the hand of the one facing west. According to one view, he takes the hand of the one facing east; according to another, he faces west while the other faces east. Then, the one who gives the directions fills their joined palms with water, and from his own joined palms, he pours water into the other's joined palms, saying: "May the divine waters be auspicious for our aid and for our drinking."

"May peace and prosperity flow toward us. Then, with his own right hand, he takes hold of the student's right hand—over the thumb and over the hair—with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take your hand with my hand; impelled by Savitṛ, who is your name? The other replies, "I am so-and-so. Having grasped his name, he murmurs: "So-and-so has taken your hand; Agni is your teacher. Whose religious student are you? For whom are you? For Ka are you?"

Whom shall I bring near? Let no one come to harm from the departing ones. O you who are setting forth, be steadfast and full of spirit; even the firm are immortal, and even the frail are immortal. Come, let us exert ourselves together; let us drive away death. Death does not roam here.

"I entrust you to Prāṇa, your teacher; I entrust you to Kubera, the great king; I entrust you to Takṣaka Vaiśāleya; I entrust you to Agni; I entrust you to Vāyu; I entrust you to Sūrya; I entrust you to Prajāpati. O Prajāpati, protect this one, [name]! Having thus entrusted him, he brings his arm down along his right shoulder toward the region of the navel and touches it, saying: "The youth, well-clad and enveloped, has come; he indeed becomes more excellent."

"Being born, the wise poets, seeking the gods with their minds and with devotion, lead him forward. Then he murmurs into his right ear: "Bhūḥ! I place thee in Bhūḥ; bhuvaḥ! I place thee in bhuvaḥ"; and into the left ear: "suvaḥ! I place thee in suvaḥ. Or rather, he may do so twice in the left ear and once in the right. Then he makes him step upon a stone with the mantra: "Step upon this stone; like a stone, be thou firm. Crush those who seek to harm us; overcome those who attack us. Then...

He causes him to place a fuel-stick on the fire with the formula: "I have brought a fuel-stick for Agni, the great Jātavedas; as you, O Agni, are kindled by the fuel-stick, so may you cause me to prosper with long life, splendor, gain, wisdom, offspring, cattle, Vedic luster, and the enjoyment of food—Svāhā! He places one stick; some say three, others seven. Having circumambulated the fire from left to right, having turned toward the north from the south, and having sat down and clasped [the teacher's feet], he asks. 8.

"Sir, recite the Sāvitrī for me. To him he recites the Sāvitrī verse foot by foot: "Bhūr, tat savitur vareṇyam; bhuvo, bhargo devasya dhīmahi; suvaḥ, dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt. Then a second time, two *vyāhṛtis* and the Sāvitrī verse half-verse by half-verse. Then a third time, all the *vyāhṛtis* and the Sāvitrī verse without pausing. Some say it should be for one who is facing westward. Regarding this Sāvitrī, some say it should be learned after a year, some after twelve nights, some after three nights, and some immediately.

Some first cause him to partake of the sacrificial cakes for the *puroḍāśa* offerings; then, handing him a staff, they say: "You are a student (*brahmacārin*); kindle the sacred fires; drink water; perform your duties; do not sleep during the day; go on alms-round; remain dependent upon your teacher; study the Veda. They say that he should eat only water at the teacher's house—this is one view; another view is that he may eat as he pleases. Thus says Bhāradvāja, the descendant of Śālmalī-mūla, or rather, they prescribe this as the ancient Vedic studentship (*vedabrahmacarya*) for forty-eight years.

Regarding this, some say [the teacher should wait] until the completion of the Vedic study; others say until the *godāna* ceremony. Then, taking hold of him by the right hand, he makes him stand up with the words, "With life, with good life! He causes him to gaze at the sun with the verse: "That eye, beneficial to the gods, which shines white in the east—may we see for a hundred autumns, may we live for a hundred autumns, may we rejoice for a hundred autumns, may we be glad for a hundred autumns, may we exist for a hundred autumns, may we hear for a hundred autumns, may we speak for a hundred autumns, may we remain unconquered for a hundred autumns, and may we long behold the sun. 9.

Then he begs for what he thinks will not be refused; having brought that and set it down, he says to the teacher, "I beg three times, or an unlimited amount. For three nights, he eats food free from pungent or salty seasoning and sleeps on the ground. Then, on the fourth day, they perform the *medhājanana* (production of intelligence) for him. Having cleared around a single-rooted *palāśa* tree that faces either the east or the north, and having washed it, he anoints it with clarified butter while moving clockwise and mutters: "O you who are well-hearing, make me well-hearing, just as you are well-hearing."

"O thou of good fame, even so make me of good fame, as thou art of good fame among the gods. "May I become a guardian of the treasure of the Vedas among the Brāhmaṇas, just as thou art a guardian of the treasure of the Vedas among the gods. Then they perform the *godāna* ceremony for him when he is sixteen years old; its ritual procedure is explained by that of the *caula*. The difference is this: he has all his hair shaved off; he gives a cow as a choice gift to the teacher; prior to the *godāna* rite, he does not bring water for bathing nor perfumes; having performed the *godāna*, he observes celibacy for one year, or he becomes one whose *godāna* is the fire. 10.

There are four grounds for marriage: wealth, beauty, wisdom, and kinship. If one cannot possess all of these, one should set aside wealth. Then there is a dispute between beauty, wisdom, and kinship; some say that one should set aside kinship, for what communion can there be with one who lacks wisdom? Now, this is another point: she is certainly not married for the sake of material wealth; rather, the primary purpose regarding her is procreation. Therefore, he who is capable of discerning [her qualities] should marry her, so that excellent offspring may be born of her.

One should take hold of her while she is sleeping, not when she is walking. When approaching her for the first time, he should ask about auspicious omens. He should bring four clods of earth: one from a sacrificial altar (*vedi*), one from a cow-dung heap, one from a furrow (*sītā*), and one from a cemetery. He says to her, "Take one of these. If she takes the clod from the sacrificial altar, he should know that she will give birth to a son who is a teacher and a performer of sacrifices. If she takes the clod from the cow-dung heap, he should know that she will give birth to a son with many cattle. If she takes the clod from the furrow, he should know that she will give birth to a son who prospers through agriculture. If she takes... [the clod from the cemetery... he should know that she will give birth to a son who follows the ways of the dead.

One should know that a clod of earth from a cemetery or a flame from a cremation fire is called "destructive"; one should not accept such a girl. Furthermore, there are many auspicious marks (*lakṣaṇa*). Regarding this, those who study marks cite a verse: "She in whom the mind finds delight and whose eyes are pleasing—one should know her to be possessed of meritorious fortune; what would one achieve by [mere] knowledge? One should accept her during the northern course of the sun (*udagayana*), for it is known that the northern course belongs to the gods; moreover, this rite is divine.

Furthermore, it is understood that the "southern course" (dakṣiṇāyana) belongs to the ancestors; thus, this rite associated with the ancestors should be undertaken during the first fortnight (pūrvapakṣa). Furthermore, it is understood that the "first fortnight" belongs to the gods; thus, this rite associated with the gods [should be undertaken during the second fortnight]. Furthermore, it is understood that the "second fortnight" (aparapakṣa) belongs to the ancestors; thus, this rite associated with the ancestors should be undertaken in the forenoon (pūrvāhṇa). Furthermore, it is understood that the "forenoon" belongs to the gods; thus, this rite associated with the gods should be undertaken at midday. It is further understood [that the afternoon belongs to the ancestors].

"Midday belongs to the Ṛṣis"—thus this rite is connected with the Ṛṣis; furthermore, it is known that therefore all merits are concentrated at midday. "The afternoon belongs to the Pitṛs"—thus this rite is connected with the Pitṛs; furthermore, it is known that [the time] is the afternoon of Bhaga; thus this rite is connected with Bhaga; furthermore, it is known that therefore maidens, desiring fortune (bhaga), move about in the afternoon. [This is] the auspicious day.

Indeed, in this world, people desire to perform their rites only on an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*); therefore, one should not dwell in nor sacrifice under a constellation with an inauspicious name, for it is declared that "whatever one does on an inauspicious day is exactly like that. An inauspicious day is indeed recognized by some as being characterized by the *inva* constellations; under these, they are sent away. Under the *maghā* constellations, cattle are seized; under the two *phalgunī*s, the army is arrayed. It is declared: "If one desires that a daughter should be beloved, one should give her away under the *niṣṭyā* (śatabhiṣaj) constellation; she becomes beloved indeed, and moreover, she does not return [to her father's house]. 12.

Then he says, "Bathe her. To her who has been bathed, he gives two garments with [the mantra]: "The goddesses who cut, who spun, who wove, and who placed the borders all around—you, O goddesses, clothe her for old age; being long-lived, put on this garment. Then he causes her to put it on with [the mantra]: "Clothe her, dress her in a garment; make her one who lives a hundred years, grant her long life. Bṛhaspati hands over this garment for King Soma to put on."

"You are going to old age; put on the garment. Become the protector against the curse of the people. Live for a hundred autumns with great luster, and clothe yourself in the increase of wealth. With these words, he consecrates her as she puts it on: "You have put this garment on for well-being; you have become the protector against the curse of the waters."

"Live a hundred autumns, O Punarṣu; living, may you distribute the riches of the noble. Then, having kindled the fire in front of her kinsmen's house, he pours the two libations (*āghāra*) and offers the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*): "To Agni, the knower of births, svāhā!"—thus in the eastern part of the northern half; "To Soma, the knower of births, svāhā!"—thus in the eastern part of the southern half. Thereafter, he offers these oblations: "Bhūḥ svāhā! Bhuvaḥ svāhā! Suvaḥ svāhā! Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ svāhā!"

Having offered the Jaya, Abhyātāna, and Rāṣṭrabhṛt oblations with the verses, "She who is transverse, she who is longitudinal," "To Saṃrādhani and Prasādhanī," and "O Jātavedas, being yoked, carry [the offering] to Sadasaspati," he offers these oblations. 13.

May Agni come first among the deities; may he release her offspring from the noose of death. May King Varuṇa grant his approval for this, so that this woman shall not weep over the calamity of losing a grandson—*svāhā*. May Agni Gārhapatya protect her; may he lead her offspring to a long life. May she have a living mother with a non-empty lap; may she awaken to the joy of seeing her grandson—*svāhā*. Let no cry of lamentation rise in your house at night; let those who weep settle elsewhere than here.

Do not, O woman with disheveled hair, strike at your breast; as the wife of a living husband, shine in the world of your lord, beholding your offspring with a joyful mind—*svāhā*. May Heaven protect your back, Vāyu your thighs, and may the Aśvins protect the suckling breast. Until the putting on of the garment, may Bṛhaspati and the Viśve Devas protect you from behind—*svāhā*. [May they destroy] childlessness, the death of sons, evil, and indeed affliction.

"Having cast off the noose from my head like a garland, I cast it upon my enemies; Svāhā! With these words, he offers a full oblation. Then, having offered the final oblation with the verses "This prayer to Varuṇa," "For this I entreat thee," "Thou, O Agni, be our nearest friend," "So thou, O Agni," "O Agni, thou art Ayāsya," "And thou, O Agni, art Ayāsya, free from curses," and "Whatever I have done in excess in this rite, O Prajāpati," he gives a choice gift to his teacher.

To the west of the fire, he spreads two sets of *darbha* grass, one set facing east and the other facing west, with their tips pointing north. Upon these, the two stand, one facing east and the other facing west; according to one view, he should take her hand while facing east, and according to another, while facing west. Then, the officiant fills their joined palms with water, and pours water from his own palm into hers, saying: "May the divine waters be auspicious for our aid and for our drink."

"May they flow toward us for our well-being and prosperity. Then, with his right hand, he takes her right hand—with the thumb facing inward and the fingers directed toward the hair—saying: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan; I take your hand with my hand for the sake of good fortune, so that you may reach old age with me as your husband. Bhaga, Aryaman, and Savitṛ, the wise ones, have given you, as a wife, to me."

Be not terrible of eye, nor a slayer of thy husband; be auspicious to cattle, most peaceful to offspring. With razor-edged [glance], O Jāra, be a mother of living sons and a bearer of heroes; be pleasant to me, O Goddess, for the sake of the household-fire, so the gods have said. O Pūṣan, send us that most auspicious woman in whom men sow their seed. She who comes to us desiring us, and in whom we, desiring her, may strike our member—Soma first obtained her, then Gandharva, and after him Agni was your third husband; the fourth of you is born of man.
Soma gave [her] to the Gandharva; the Gandharva gave [her] to Agni;
Agni gave [her] to me, as well as wealth and sons. O Sarasvatī, O fortunate one, rich in sacrificial food, protect this [woman] here.

"We shall sing aloud to you, the foremost of all that exists. Then the Brahman priest consecrates the two with the mantra: "Be united; may your hearts be in accord. May your minds be joined together; may your breath be joined together. Then he makes her step upon a stone with the words: "Step upon this stone; like a stone, be firm. Crush those who seek to harm us; overcome those who attack us. He leads her around the fire clockwise, [saying]: "And through you, may we overcome all [enemies], as one overcomes streams of water."

"May we overcome our enemies. Then her brother, with his own joined palms, pours into her palms the parched grains (*lāja*) that have been spread out and sprinkled with clarified butter, while she recites: "This woman, as she offers the parched grains into the fire, prays: 'May my husband be long-lived; may my kinsmen prosper. I unite you with fortune, like wine with *māsara*. " Then he makes her say: "I pour these parched grains, which bring about prosperity, for myself and for your union; may Agni approve this, Svāhā! In this same manner, he causes her to stand three times, leads her around three times, and pours the grains three times; then he leads her either eastward or northward.

He causes her to take seven steps, muttering at the seventh step while looking at her: "One step for food—may Viṣṇu follow you; two for strength—may Viṣṇu follow you; three for sacred vows—may Viṣṇu follow you; four for comfort—may Viṣṇu follow you; five for cattle—may Viṣṇu follow you; six for the increase of wealth—may Viṣṇu follow you; seven for the seven priestly offices—may Viṣṇu follow you. He says: "Become my friend by these seven steps; we have become friends by these seven steps."

"May I attain friendship with you; may I not be separated from your friendship; may you not be separated from my friendship. Then, having drawn his arm across her right shoulder down to the region of her heart, he touches her heart, saying: "May your heart be in my heart; may your mind be in my mind. Listen to my word with an undivided mind; be devoted to me alone; be my companion through life. Then he whispers into her right ear: "May my mind enter into yours; may my sight [enter] you; may my mind [enter] you."
May all beings be in me; may your wisdom be in me.
O Honey! I plunge into honey. Let my tongue be a speaker of honey; let there be the honey of the bees in my mouth; let the charm of conciliation be placed in those who eat.
"The enchantment of the cakravāka birds which has been brought forth from the rivers—that which the gods and gandharvas know—by that we two are united.
Behold me and behold the sun; do not set your heart on others. 17

Then, holding an axe upon her head, he sprinkles gold or water from a water-pot with the three verses beginning "O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss," with the four verses beginning "Gold-colored, pure, purifying," and with the entire section beginning "Pavamāna, [belonging to] the world of light. Having sprinkled her, they carry her away as is appropriate; while she is being carried, he addresses her with the mantra: "The two who carry the bride's splendor—the consumption-diseases that follow after people."

"May those gods worthy of sacrifice lead them back from whence they came"—having said this, he causes her to be carried to the house and makes her sit down upon the hide of a red bull with the words: "Here let the cows settle; here the horses, here the men."

"May Pūṣan, accompanied by a thousand sacrificial fees, sit down here"—having said this, he then causes her to sacrifice with a *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice offering) dedicated to Agni. Then, having taken a portion of this *sthālīpāka* and poured clarified butter over it, he offers it, saying: "To Agni, Svāhā! To Agni with his fires, Svāhā! To Agni, the eater of food, Svāhā! To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, Svāhā! For as long as he lives, he serves this fire every morning and evening with rice or barley. In the evening, he offers the first oblation with "To Agni, Svāhā! and the second with "To Prajāpati, Svāhā! The first [oblation] belongs to Sūrya.

Some authorities prescribe that [the fire] should be maintained daily from the morning; if it goes out, it should either be churned or fetched from the house of a Śrotriya, and for one of these two options, there is fasting on that day.

He observes fasts on the eighth days and on the festival days (parvan). On the festival days, he sacrifices with a *sthālīpāka* offering dedicated to Agni. Remaining silent, he sits until the rising of the stars; when the stars have risen, having taken hold of the calf, he makes it rise with the mantra: "Up with life, up with good life! Then he causes her to look at the Pole Star (*dhruva*), Arundhatī, and other stars. He worships the Pole Star with this section: "Homage to Brahman, the Pole Star, the unshakable! You are the Pole Star, you are of firm origin, you are the Pole Star, established by the Pole Star."
"You are the pivot of the constellations; as such, protect me from those who attack. Thus did the Seven Seers first lead Arundhatī, the steadfast one among the Kṛttikās.

"May this eighth day shine for us, during which the six Kṛttikās maintain their primary conjunction"—having said this, the two [the husband and wife] remain for three nights as celibates, sleeping on the ground and eating food free from pungent spices and salt. Then, on the fourth night, in the latter part of the night, having established the fire in the inner chamber and offered the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations, he offers these oblations: "O Agni, you are the expiation; you are the expiation of the gods. I, a Brāhmaṇa seeking protection, approach you."

Whatever body of hers is husband-slaying, offspring-slaying, cattle-slaying, or fortune-slaying—I make that one her lover-slaying; *svāhā*! O Vāyu, you are the expiation; O Āditya, you are the expiation; O Prajāpati, you are the expiation. You are the expiation of the gods; I, a Brāhmaṇa seeking protection, take refuge in you. Whatever despised body she has, we cause that to perish from here; *svāhā*. 19.

Then, having uttered the *hiṃ* sound silently, he approaches her while restraining his speech, saying: "I am the sky, you are the earth; I am the Sāman, you are the Ṛc; come, let us two unite; let us both deposit seed for the sake of obtaining a male son, for the increase of wealth, for good progeny, and for heroic vigor. Then, when she has finished her purpose and he has finished his purpose, he places his mouth near her mouth and breathes out upon her, saying: "Breathe out this breath. She then breathes in toward him. Then, after she has sipped water and washed her hands, he touches her.

"May I touch you with my auspicious hand, which has five fingers, which is free from enmity, powerful, and glorious, for the sake of good progeny"—with these words he touches her in the region of the buttocks. When she is in her courses, he then instructs her in the observances forbidden by the Brāhmaṇas, beginning with the verse, "Her who is in her courses... On the fourth day, when she has bathed, is wearing clean clothes, and has conversed with a Brāhmaṇa, he lies down with her with this Anuvāka, "May your mind unite with my mind. According to Āśmarathya, all the acts of approaching are accompanied by mantras; according to Ālekhana, they are so only at the beginning and at the end. 20.

Now, in the fourth month of her first pregnancy, they perform the *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair) during the waxing fortnight under an auspicious constellation. Having cooked a *sthālīpāka* (oblation of rice) in milk, and having established the fire in the inner chamber, he offers the *jayā*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations, and then offers these following oblations: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ Prajāpate. With a porcupine quill having three white spots, having brought forward three bunches of *darbha* grass and a handful of *śalālu* fruit, he parts the hair upwards with the formula: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ; I [invoke] Rākā..."

"O Rākā, those [powers] of yours... "Soma alone is our king," so say the Brāhmaṇa women, sitting with their wheels turned back, on the bank of the Yamunā, saying, "On your bank, O Yamunā! Or rather, "On your bank," referring to whichever bank she dwells upon. Having placed these [offerings] to the east of the fire, he draws out three portions of boiled rice, sprinkles them with clarified butter, and sets them down, with a vessel of water as the fourth. As they gaze at each of these one by one, he asks, "What do you see? They reply, "Sons and cattle. Of these, he should feed one portion to Brāhmaṇas, one to Brāhmaṇa women, and one to...
Together with the boys, she eats; she remains silent until the rising of the stars; when the stars have risen—the rest is the same. 21.

Now, the *puṃsavana* rite is performed in the third month, or at the beginning of the fourth, under the asterism Tiṣya, or Hasta, or Anurādhā, or the Uttarā-proṣṭhapadas. Having fetched a shoot from the root of a *nyagrodha* tree, it is ground with a stone on a stone by a maiden who has not yet bathed after her menses. Then, having established the fire in the inner chamber and offered the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations, he offers these following oblations: the four verses beginning with "He who [knows] thee with the heart and the mind," and so forth. To the west of the fire, having laid her down facing east with her face upward, he then [places the mixture] upon her right [side].

He inserts his thumb into the nostril [of the woman] with the formula, "This is the male-procreation for such-and-such a person"; she says, "So be it," and thus she gives birth to a male child. Now, for the quick delivery: having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavīta), having sipped water, and having brought water from a flowing stream in an unbaked earthen bowl, he places the woman, who is groaning, upon her back and touches her head while she is perspiring, with ten fingers, saying: "With ten fingers I touch thee, so that thou mayest give birth after ten months. Then he sprinkles her with water, saying: "As the wind blows, as the ocean surges..."

"Thus, O boy, move together with the afterbirth; fall away! Then, if it does not fall away, he should take water in his hand and sprinkle it on her head, saying: "Fall away like sesame seeds! You are not flesh, you are not a leaf; fall away, so-and-so! If the fetus should become detached, he should stroke it three times upward from the navel with a moist hand, saying: "May Tvaṣṭṛ bind you with bonds—away from me, not toward me. Wait for the seasons, for ten months, as one who does not slay heroes. (22)

For a woman who has given birth, he performs the rite of protection (*paridā*). Having kindled a fire in the southern part of the house and having poured mustard seeds mixed with *phalīkaraṇa* grains into his joined palms, he offers them as oblations, saying: "Śaṇḍa, Marka, Upavīra, Tuṇḍikera, Ulūkhala—let Cyavana perish from here, Svāhā! He does so a second time and likewise a third time. Then another [verse]: "Keśinī, Śvalominī, Khajā, Bījopakāśinī."

"Depart! Perish from here, svāhā!"—thus the second [offering], and thus the third. Then another: "The one with a jar-vessel, the vessel-in-hand, the skillful servant of Aryaman; depart! Perish from here, svāhā!"—thus the second, and thus the third. Then another: "The Kauberakas, dressed in mixed garments, sent by the King of the Rākṣasas; they go to the village with their kin, seeking those who have not performed the funeral rites, svāhā! Slay these! Seize these!"—this is the Brāhmaṇa messenger. Agni went around them, Indra went around them, and Bṛhaspati went around them.

I, a Brahmin, know them as they feel about them: those with false teeth, disheveled hair, and hanging breasts—*svāhā*! Those who wander by night, breast-bearers, spear-handed, and skull-drinkers; among them, the father goes first, loud-eared so that he may hear; the mother creeps behind, seeking a lonely man in the village—*svāhā*! The sister who wanders at twilight looks into the family through a crack; she who wakes the sleeping one, whose mind is set upon her when she has given birth.

"O Agni, for those [women], burn their lungs, heart, liver, and eyes with your black path; Svāhā!"—in this very manner he scatters [the grains] as she goes out and as she enters, day after day, until the ten-day period has passed. 23.

If she gives birth to a male child, he touches him with the formula "Growing" (*vṛdhat*). Having wrapped the middle leaf of a *palāśa* tree, he murmurs into his right ear: "Bhūḥ, I place thee in me; bhuvaḥ, I place thee in me; suvaḥ, I place thee in me. Or rather, [he murmurs] into the left ear twice, and once into the right. Then he addresses him with the mantra: "Be a stone, be an axe, be unassailable gold. Thou art indeed the Veda named 'son'; live a hundred autumns!"

"May the god Savitṛ bestow wisdom upon you; may the goddess Sarasvatī bestow wisdom upon you; may both the Aśvins, garlanded with lotuses, bestow wisdom upon you. You are indeed the Veda named 'Son'; live for a hundred autumns. Then, having mixed together curds, honey, and ghee, he causes him to eat it three times with three bunches of *darbha* grass or with gold, [reciting]: "I cause you to eat the essence of the waters and of the plants; I bestow upon you long life, splendor, glory, and wisdom. Impelled by Savitṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ has placed the hero within you; may you be one who lives a hundred years for me."

With the words "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he then takes hold of the boy's right hand with his own right hand—grasping it over the thumb and over the hairs—with these mantras beginning "Agni is long-lived"; having anointed both hands with fresh butter and having placed a piece of gold in the boy's hand. 24.

Having warmed it over the fire, he touches it with: "I touch you with the brilliance of Agni, with the splendor of Sūrya, with the power of Indra, with the will of all the gods. You arise from limb after limb; you are born from the heart. You are indeed the self named 'son'; live a hundred autumns! Then he touches him with the Vātsapra hymn, with the section beginning "From heaven," and he touches the spot where he lies with: "I know your heart, O Earth; it rests in the sky in the moon."

"May I not weep over the sin against my grandson, the protector of the nectar of the Vedas. Then he places him in his mother's lap with the verse: "May no *rakṣas* slay your son; may she not be a cow that has strayed too far. May she be dear to wealth, prospering in her own domain. He causes him to suckle at the breast with the verse: "May this boy suckle for long life; may he attain old age."

Saying, "Swell for him the breast with life, luster, fame, and strength," he performs the entrustment for the two women who have lain down together; she neither cries out nor weeps. Saying, "Wherever we speak and wherever we touch," he places a water-pot at her head. He says, "O Waters, be watchful while they sleep; drive away the demons from here. They do not use these waters for the purpose of drinking. Now, if she does not give birth for a long time, one should show her a wreath; once she is delivered, one should quickly carry her out whenever [the need arises].

In the case of puerperal fever (sūtikā-roga), one should moisten the heel of the right foot with hot water and repeatedly rub that spot where she experiences pain. [One should recite: "The bow and the quiver are in the hands of the man; a hundredfold is your power. O limb, you rule over disease; you rule over health. You are the remedy for puerperal fever for this woman, so-and-so. 25.

They carry out the birth-fire (*sūtikāgni*) and they bring forward the domestic fire (*aupāsana*). This [birth-fire] is for the purpose of heating; no ritual action whatsoever is performed in it. On the tenth day, having bathed, the mother and son prepare a pure chamber; they carry out the domestic fire and bring forward the birth-fire. Having kindled the fire in the inner chamber and offered the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations, he offers these oblations: "May Dhātṛ grant us wealth," and so forth, eight [times]. On the tenth day, he gives a name to the son, consisting of two syllables.

Or [the name] should consist of four syllables, beginning with a sonant, containing a semivowel (*antastha*), and ending with a long vowel or a visarga (*abhiniṣṭāna*); for it is known that "this is firmly established. First, the father and mother should utter [the name], as it is known: "O Jātavedas, my first name was what my father and mother bestowed at the beginning. He should give him two names; for it is known: "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa who has two names prospers. The second name should be that of a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*); one of them should be secret, and they should address him by the other. 26.

Having stayed away, the doe, having taken dūrvā grass, approaches the house: "O House, do not fear; do not tremble! Bearing strength, we come to you. Bearing strength, well-disposed and full of luster, I approach the house with a joyful mind. Those houses for whose sake one who is traveling abroad longs, and in which there is much goodwill—those houses we invoke; may they recognize us as we recognize them. These houses stand firm among the living, bearing strength, most gracious to the world."

Let this calf low, and let the young bull come; let the many cows, whose calves are ever-present, approach. Cattle and horses are invited; goats and sheep are invited. And may the sweet essence of food be invited into my house.

"Bearing strength, come hither; I unite you with strength; rest, do not fear," with these words he throws grass [into the fire]. "May they be auspicious for the one who approaches and for the one who departs," with this he touches the two doorposts. "For your security, I enter the auspicious one for peace," with this he enters. He gazes toward the south-east. "May there be safety for you; may there be safety for me," with this he addresses his wife as they are uniting. With the verse, "And all things by thee," he addresses the son.

He consecrates the child as it is being united [with the mother] with two verses beginning, "From limb by limb you are born. Then he should smell him on the head three times, saying: "I smell you with the *hiṃkāra* of cattle; I smell you with the *hiṃkāra* of Prajāpati. May Prajāpati grant you life; may you live a hundred years for me. Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! You are born from all the vital breaths; live a hundred autumns! This is for a daughter. Then, in the sixth month, he feeds him solid food. For that, the same ritual procedure for feeding applies which was prescribed for the son.
In the rite for generating intelligence (*medhājanana*), there is this much difference: he causes [the child] to eat [the food] first with "Bhūḥ," second with "Bhuvaḥ," and third with "Suvaḥ. 27.

Then, when he is one year old, they perform the *caula* ceremony for him, according to his lineage (*ṛṣi*) or according to the specific tradition of his family. It is known from the Vedic texts: "Where the arrows fly together like boys with their hair-locks"—meaning those with many locks. Then, having prepared food and fed the Brahmins, and having caused them to pronounce blessings, he kindles the fire in the inner chamber. Having offered the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations, he offers these following oblations: *pūrṇā*, *paścāt*, *imaṃ me varuṇa*, *tattvā yāmi*, *tvaṃ no agne*, and *sa tvaṃ no agne*.

"O Agni, you who are tireless, [protect us] from curses; whatever of this rite I have done in excess, O Prajāpati," having offered this final oblation, he gives a choice gift to the teacher. To the west of the fire, having placed a ball of cow-dung and all kinds of seeds nearby, and having poured the finest portion of all the seeds onto the ball of cow-dung, and having brought together water that is both cold and warm, he moistens his right godāna (the hair at the side of the head) with that water, saying: "May the waters moisten [you] for life, for long life, and for luster. Having removed three hairs with a porcupine quill that has three white spots, he discards them.

He places bundles of *darbha* grass with their tips pointing upwards, saying, "O herb, protect him! O razor, do not harm him! Having placed a red iron razor across [the hair], he shaves it, saying: "The triple life-span of the seers, the triple life-span of Jamadagni and Kaśyapa, the triple life-span of the gods—may that triple life-span be mine."

"With that by which Pūṣan shaved the hair for the sake of the long life of Bṛhaspati, Agni, and Indra—with that I shave you, O [Name], for long life and luster. In this very manner he has the hair on the other side shaved. Having had the hair shaved, he places it upon a lump of cow-dung. Then he places that lump of cow-dung in a cow-pen, at the edge of water, at the root of an Udumbara tree, or at a clump of Darbha grass.
Then they adorn him after he has been bathed.
Thus ends the first book in the Bhāradvāja Sūtra.

We shall now explain the ritual of the Śravaṇa ceremony. On the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one prepares unhusked grains, parched grain-flour, and genuine collyrium. After the sun has set, having established the fire within the inner chamber and offered the Jaya, Abhyātāna, and Rāṣṭrabhṛt oblations, he takes portions of both the unhusked grains and the parched grain-flour, sprinkles them with clarified butter, and offers the first oblation with the mantra: "To Agni Pāṇḍara, the lord of earthly beings, svāhā! He then offers [the second] to Śveta...

With the words, "Svāhā to Vāyu, the lord of the intermediate spaces," he offers the second oblation; with "Svāhā to Sūrya, the conqueror, the lord of the heavens," the third. Having gone outside, he offers these oblations upon a leveled mound (*sthaṇḍila*). Alternatively, having prepared parched grains (*dhānā*) for the purpose of eating—along with uncrushed grains, flour of uncrushed grains, and collyrium of the *jātya* variety—and having placed them on the leveled mound, he consecrates them with the three verses beginning, "Homage be to the serpents. Then, he [covers] as much space as he desires.

Thinking, "Lest these serpents should come here," he sprinkles it all around with a continuous stream of water, [chanting]: "O White One, strike them down with your foot, both from the front and from behind—with the seven sons of Manu and these three kinsmen of the King! Indeed, in the domain of the White One, no serpent has ever bitten anyone."

"Salutation to Śveta Vaidarvya"—saying this, as many as there are who desire to eat the remains of the sacrificial oblation, they gather and swallow these parched grains (dhānā). Then, for these four months, they offer an oblation (bali) to the serpents; they prepare either groats (saktu) or whatever other food is prepared.

Then, on the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī, this very same ritual is performed—everything except for the eating of parched grains and the sprinkling around. On the festival days (parvan), he sacrifices with a *sthālīpāka* offering dedicated to Agni; prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation of that sacrifice, he offers these oblations: "O Jātavedas, enjoy this oblation, the footprint of Iḍā, rich in ghee, moving and unmoving. May there be delight here for the nourishment of those seven domestic animals of all forms. Svāhā! To the night which the gods welcome like a cow approaching..."
She who is the wife of the year, may she be auspicious for us; Svāhā!
The Full Moon, fulfilling [the cycle], comes again and again, dividing the half-months; may she protect us with her fullness; Svāhā!
"Auspicious to our cattle, auspicious to our wives, auspicious by night, auspicious by day, fashioning the year—may she be a cow of plenty for us, svāhā!
O Agni, thou art the full one in the west; O Prajāpati, thou art the leader. Then he offers three oblations with these verses, and thereafter he makes the offering to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.

"To Sviṣṭakṛt, Svāhā! Then, at the time when he is about to descend for the winter solstice (*hemantapratyavarohaṇa*), he worships [the earth] with: "I find firm footing in the ruling power, I find firm footing in the kingdom; I find firm footing in horses, I find firm footing in cattle; I find firm footing in offspring, in what is to be. O Earth, be pleasant to us, thornless, a place of rest; grant us wide protection. (2)

We shall now explain the rite of the house-consecration (*śālākarma*). One who intends to have a house built, during the waxing fortnight under an auspicious lunar mansion, having served food to the Brahmins and having drawn a line around the site, [recites]: "Right here I fix the firm foundation; may the house stand secure, dripping with clarified butter. Into thee, O House, may we all enter, accompanied by heroes, possessing heroes, and with our heroes unharmed. With these words, he erects the southern door-post. [He continues]: "O House, be thou firmly established right here, rich in horses, rich in cattle, and full of pleasant speech."

"Full of vigor, full of milk, full of ghee, rise up for great good fortune!"—with these words he raises the northern post. "May the young boy come to you, may the calf with the moving world come to you; may the jar of flowing liquor and the pots of curd come to you"—with these words he touches the two posts when they are joined together. In this very same way he raises the two chief pillars and touches them: "By means of Truth, ascend the pillar, O beam; being fierce and shining forth, drive away the enemies."

Then he places her upon the back of the cart, saying: "May you grant us wealth consisting of all heroes. He touches her while she is covered, saying: "O mistress of the mind, be a refuge, be pleasant; you have been measured out by the gods in the beginning. Wearing grass, well-disposed, you have sat down; be auspicious to us, be auspicious to our bipeds, be auspicious to our quadrupeds. (3)

We shall explain the entry into the house. During the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, having established the fire within the inner chamber and offered the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations, he offers these following oblations: "O Lord of the Dwelling (*vāstoṣpati*), two [verses]: 'O Lord of the Dwelling, be our furtherer; O Indu, increase our wealth in cattle and horses. May we remain unaging in your friendship; as a father his sons, favor us. *Svāhā!* 'O Death, go away along your own path, which is other than that traveled by the gods.'"

"O Vāstoṣpati, I speak to you who hears us: do not harm our offspring, nor our men—Svāhā! With these words he touches the ground. Then, with the two verses beginning "I stand firm in my power, I stand firm in my kingdom," and "This is a better dwelling-place than I came to; for me, Heaven and Earth have become pleasant," [he settles].

First, the pacification of the site (*vāstu-śamana*) is performed; then, another rite is done in the dwelling. One takes hollowed-out *udumbara* and *palāśa* leaves along with barley, cow-dung, grass from a meadow (*śāḍvala*), a donkey, and honey as the seventh item. With these, one should sprinkle the house and the site. A full vessel of water is placed there, and a fire is kindled. He causes a Brāhmaṇa to enter first. He says to the Brāhmaṇa, "May you enter. [The Brāhmaṇa replies: "May your honor enter, endowed with long life, splendor, and prosperity. Having been permitted by the Brāhmaṇa, he enters, saying: "I resort to *bhūḥ*; I resort to *bhuvaḥ*."

"I take refuge in Śrī; I take refuge in Śrī; may Śrī enter me"—having thus entered after the Brāhmaṇa, and having offered the *jayas*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*, he magnifies Agni, the god of the gods: "Agni is the overlord of the gods, the one who dwells in the soil, the bearer of oblations. To him, O God, I go for refuge, together with my sons, together with the wise, together with my wife, together with my kinsmen, together with my attendants; to Agni, svāhā! Having thus magnified Agni, he then praises the King: "Indeed, the strength given by you is in the kingdom; through your bounty one lives here."

"Hiraṇyavarṇa, haryakṣa, accomplish my purpose, svāhā! To Kubera, svāhā! To the Great King, svāhā! To Vaiśravaṇa, svāhā! Having thus magnified the King, he then magnifies Indra, the lord of the gods, with the verses "Indra is our protector" and "All have magnified Indra. Having thus magnified Indra, he magnifies the Viśvedevas with the two verses "O Viśvedevas" and "The Viśvedevas. Having thus magnified the Viśvedevas... 5.

Then, having added five fuel-sticks, he offers oblations: "I offer intelligence into the mind, Svāhā! I offer the mind into intelligence, Svāhā! I offer faith into austerity, Svāhā! I offer austerity into faith, Svāhā! I place [this] within the mouth of Death, Svāhā! The gods who dwell in the east, led by Agni, slayers of demons—may they protect us, may they aid us; homage to them, Svāhā! I enter this peaceful conclusion, Svāhā!"

The gods who sit on the south, the gods who sit on the west, the gods who sit on the north, and the gods who sit above—those slayers of Rākṣasas led by Bṛhaspati—may they protect us, may they aid us; homage to them, svāhā! I enter this peaceful dwelling, svāhā!

Having offered the *pūrṇā* oblation last, [with the verses] "O Varuṇa, this for me," "To you I go," "You, O Agni, for us," "So you, O Agni, for us," "You, O Agni, are Ayāsya," "And you, O Agni, are Ayāsya," "And [grant] freedom from curses," and "Whatever I have done in excess of this rite, O Prajāpati"—having offered the final oblation with these, he should serve food to the Brāhmaṇas. Wherever the site is censurable, or wherever another might prevail, there too he should dwell in comfort, pacifying the site. This is the word of Dhaumya, of the sage Asita Turaṅga, and of Kāvya Dālbhya:
one who knows this shall not suffer defeat. 6.

The expiation for being touched by a dog: having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (yajñopavīta), sipped water, and brought water from a stream in a vessel that has not been consecrated with the *āprī* verses, he then clears a space for gambling in the middle of the assembly hall, sprinkles it, scatters dice upon it, places gold among the dice, spreads grass over the assembly hall, and leads the boy along with it. Having laid the boy down supine upon the dice and sprinkled him with curds mixed with salt water, he mutters: "They strike the bronze; Kurkura, Sukurkura, Kurkura, the binder of children;
that which was born above in the third heaven from here."
The Aulaba, Itta, Upāhvaya, Arjīkya, Śyāma, Śabala,
Adhorāma, and Ulumbala— the dog runs forth like one gazing upon the ocean,
wearing a golden neck-ornament and a breastplate, the most vigorous at the head of the dogs.
"O Subīriṇa, release him! Release him, O Ekavrātya! O Śunaka, release him!
"That is the truth," [said Indra], "that you said, 'Let me bind him. Having bound him, you came here. He said to you, 'I have found him!

That is the truth: that Saramā is your mother and Lohita is your father;

Release this one; you are pure-minded, though you are tawny-red.

"May he desire a dog for food and a man for clothing"—reciting this three times in the morning, at midday, and in the evening, he becomes free from disease; so it is said. Therefore, one should perform this [rite] if he has not become free from disease. We shall now explain the Śūlagava sacrifice.

During the fortnight of the waxing moon, under an auspicious constellation, having cooked a *sthālīpāka* (pot-offering) of milk, and having gone out toward either the eastern or northern direction, having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and established the fire, and having strewn grass around it, one constructs two huts to the west of the fire. Then one invokes the Śūlagava with the verse: "May the well-disposed bay horses bring thee hither, together with white horses that possess banners."

With the words, "O Śarva, come for my oblation with winds as swift as a race-course," he offers to the south; to the north, the *śūlagava* (the spit-ox sacrifice); in the middle, the *mīḍhuṣī*; and [to] Jayanta. Having offered water according to the order in which they were brought, and having drawn out three portions of boiled rice, he causes them to touch [the water] in that same order: "May the Bountiful One touch it—svāhā to the Bountiful One! May the Bountiful Woman touch it—svāhā to the Bountiful Woman! O Jayanta, touch it—svāhā to Jayanta! Having carried the fire of the *śūlagava* forward, he makes offerings: "To the god Bhava, svāhā! To the god Śarva, svāhā! To the god Īśāna, svāhā!"
Svāhā to the god Ugra, svāhā to the god Bhīma, svāhā to the god Rudra, svāhā to the god Paśupati, svāhā to the great god—thus [he offers]. 8.

He offers the *patnyodana* (rice for the wives) to the wives [of the gods], saying: "Svāhā to the wife of the god Bhava; svāhā to the wife of the god Śarva; svāhā to the wife of the god Īśāna; svāhā to the wife of the god Ugra; svāhā to the wife of the god Bhīma; svāhā to the wife of the god Rudra; svāhā to the wife of the god Paśupati; svāhā to the wife of the great god. He offers the middle portion of all the *odanas* with the formula: "Svāhā to Jayanta."

Having taken portions of the food one by one and having sprinkled them with clarified butter, he offers the oblation, saying, "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, Svāhā! Then he stands in worship, saying, "May the full-faced one walk around us for our well-being. Now follows the distribution of the leaves: "House-guardian, touch! To the house-guardian, Svāhā! House-protector, touch! To the house-protector, Svāhā! Victor, touch! To the victor, Svāhā!"—thus six *palāśa* leaves. Then others: "The noisy ones, touch! To the noisy ones, Svāhā! The snorting ones, touch! To the snorting ones, Svāhā! The sorting ones, touch!"

"To those who are gathering, svāhā! Touching [the water], 'To those who are collecting, svāhā! Touching [the water], 'To those who are eating together, svāhā!'—ten [oblations]. Then others: 'O divine armies, touch [the water]! To the divine armies, svāhā!'—ten indeed. Then others: 'Those divine armies which are named and those which are unnamed, touch [the water]! To them, svāhā!'—ten indeed. (9)

Then he offers four oblations: "To the door-keeper, svāhā! Having touched the door-post, 'To the door-post, svāhā! Having made a leaf-cup, having taken a ball of cooked rice therein, over which butter has been spread and poured, he hangs it on a tree beyond the cow-pen, saying: 'To the quiver-bearers, touch [it]! To the quiver-bearers, svāhā! Then he worships, saying: 'Homage to the quiver-bearers, the ones with quivers! Without looking back, he returns; then he makes two offerings to the followers, saying: 'To the followers, touch [it]! To the followers, svāhā!'"

Then, at the *palāśa* tree, he stands in worship with these eleven sections beginning with "Homage to you, O Rudra, to your wrath," or else with the first and last [sections] on both sides; he stations the cows around this fire so that they may smell the smoke. Having poured together into one place the remnants of the clarified butter, the remnants of the cooked rice, and the remnants of the water-jar, he sprinkles the cows three times clockwise with a branch of the *udumbara* tree, saying, "Auspiciousness to the cows, auspiciousness to the lord of the cows. He pours the remainder over the back of the bull with these five verses beginning with "This youth... and then follows this:

On the path of cattle belonging to the lord of the field (*kṣetrapati*), he sacrifices to the Lord of the Field in a fireless place with the mantra, "To the Lord of the Field, svāhā! He invokes him upon four or seven *palāśa* leaves in the same manner as the *śūlagava* sacrifice. He quickly performs the sacrifice; the cooked offering stands near. With the two verses beginning, "By the Lord of the Field we... he worships. Then those who are his kinsmen eat this sacrificial portion of the Lord of the Field according to their family custom. 10.

On the new moon day, in the afternoon, or on the odd-numbered days of the dark fortnight, having prepared food for the ancestors, having arranged the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta), having kindled the fire, and having strewn darbha grass around the fire with its tips pointing south and east, he faces the intermediate direction between the south and the east and invokes the ancestors: "Come, O Soma-loving ancestors, by your deep and ancient paths; bestowing upon us progeny, wealth, and long life of a hundred autumns."

"Come, O grandfathers and great-grandfathers, together with your followers—those who are difficult to reach, united with truth, and free from cruelty. May the fathers come today to our invocation; may the fathers come here to eat the oblation. Having sprinkled water toward this very direction, he pours out water with the mantra: "O divine waters, send forth this sacrifice; may the fathers enjoy our offering. May they, and those who partake of the strength of the months, bestow upon us wealth consisting of all heroic sons. Having sprinkled around, he makes an offering with the verse: "The waters that flow eastward and those that come from the north..."

With the waters that sustain the entire world, I place an interval between [him] and the father; for such-and-such, *svāhā*! I place an interval with the mountains, with the great earth, with the sky, with the quarters, and with infinite protections; I place an interval between [him] and the grandfather; for such-and-such, *svāhā*! I place an interval with the seasons, with days and nights together with their junctions, and with half-months and months; I place an interval between [him] and the great-grandfather; for such-and-such, *svāhā*! Whatever limb of yours the flesh-eating Jātavedas has burnt while leading you toward the worlds—
Therefore, I cause you to enter [the body] again; being unharmed, be united with all your limbs, O Fathers! Svadhā! Adoration to the Fathers! Svāhā! 11.

Then he offers of the food: "Svāhā to Agni accompanied by the Pitṛs; Svāhā to Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs; Svāhā to Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the Pitṛs; Svadhā! Adoration to the Pitṛs! Svāhā! To Agni Kavyavāhana, the maker of good offerings; Svadhā! Adoration to the Pitṛs! Svāhā! Having sprinkled water around [the fire] and placed a handful of Darbha grass to the south, he pours three handfuls of water ending toward the south into it, saying: "O So-and-so, wash yourself! for the father; "O So-and-so, wash yourself! for the grandfather; "O So-and-so, wash yourself! for the great-grandfather.

At this very spot, with his right hand extended downward, he places three rice-balls (piṇḍas) ending toward the south for the great-grandfather, naming him, saying: "This, O grandfather [Name], is for you—sweet food, full of essence. As great as fire and the earth are, so great is its measure; I give this measure to you as it truly is. Just as fire is preserved and not diminished, so may it be preserved and not diminished for my father. May you become *svadhā*. Live upon this imperishable *svadhā* together with them—those whom you follow here and those who follow you."

This honeyed food for your grandfather, O Sarasvant—whatever the extent of the wind and the intermediate space, that much is its measure. I give this measure to you as it truly is. Just as the wind is undecaying and imperishable, so may it be undecaying and imperishable for me, for my grandfather. Be *svadhā* unto them; live upon that undecaying *svadhā* together with them, both those whom you support here and those who depend on you. 12.

This honeyed food for you, O great-grandfather, belongs to Sarasvant. As great as the sun and the sky are, so great is its measure; I give this measure to you as it truly is. Just as the sun is imperishable and undecaying, so may it be imperishable and undecaying for me, your great-grandfather. May you become *svadhā*; live upon that imperishable *svadhā* together with them—those whom you support here and those who follow after you.

Having said, "O fathers, enjoy according to your portions," he turns away. He waits until the heat has subsided; once the heat has subsided, he turns back. Having turned back, while [the heat] has not yet subsided, he worships with salutations, beginning with, "Obeisance to you, O fathers, the essence," and ending with, "May I become the most excellent among them. Then, having washed the vessel with water and filled it, he sprinkles it three times from right to left (prasavya), [saying], "The waters, satisfying sons and grandsons..."

"May these rivers, full of prosperity, yielding the *svadhā* offering and immortality to the ancestors, the divine waters, satisfy both [the gods and the ancestors]. Carrying strength—milk, water, ghee, milk, honey, and flowing nectar—may these rivers, full of water, rich in reeds, and possessing excellent fords, flow for you in that world. Rich in strength, rich in milk, with honey and ghee, you are the *svadhā*; satisfy my ancestors! Having approached without looking back, [he recites this]. 13.

Then he touches the food with the mantra: "The earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid; I offer you into the mouth of Brahman; I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; do not perish for them there, in yonder world. The earth is equal to it; Agni is its witness; the Ṛg-verses are its greatness. The earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid; I offer you into the mouth of Brahman; I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; do not perish for them there, in yonder world. The intermediate space is equal to it; Vāyu is its witness; the Sāman-chants are its greatness."

"The earth is your vessel, the sky is your lid; I offer you into the mouth of Brahman; I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; may you not perish among them there, in that world. The sky is its equal; the sun is its witness; the Yajus-formulas are your greatness. Having served the Brāhmaṇas with food, and having taken the vessel of water as directed, he goes to the south-eastern intermediate direction and pours out the water as directed: "Depart, O Soma-loving fathers, by deep paths..."

"By the ancient paths, come back to our house every month, to eat the oblation, with good offspring and brave heroes. Having taken portions from all [the food], he eats of the remainder, saying: "May this food be full and never-failing; may it be for us immortality together with the gods. I offer you, the immortal, into the vital breaths, svāhā! (14)

We shall explain the Aṣṭakā. After the full moon of Māgha and before the full moon of Phālguna, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight which coincides with the Jyeṣṭhā nakṣatra, they call that the Ekāṣṭakā. On that day, he prepares the ritual materials: an excellent cow and a cake for the Aṣṭakā made from four śarāvas of grain. He offers it silently; it may be prepared on six potsherds or on one potsherd. Its preparation follows the procedure for a wood-oblation (dārvihoma). Having cooked it on the Āvasathya fire, he offers it on that very Āvasathya fire. "The mortars and the pressing-stones have raised their voice, preparing the oblation."

Yearly, O Ekāṣṭakā, may we be possessed of good offspring and heroic sons, and masters of riches. *Svadhā!* Salutation to the ancestors! *Svāhā!* This cake, O Agni, prepared in four bowls, rich in ghee, rich in milk, wealthy, and full of nourishment—may the ancestors accept it in harmony. May this be well-sacrificed and well-offered for me. *Svadhā!* Salutation to the ancestors! *Svāhā!* Carry the cake, O Jātavedas, to the ancestors wherever you know them to be hidden in the distance.

"May rows of cakes flow toward them; may their blessings be true, according to their desires! *Svadhā*! *Namaḥ* to the ancestors! *Svāhā*!"—with these words he offers these oblations before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. Behind [the *sviṣṭakṛt*] he offers a full [oblation], and then three [more] with the verses, "O Agni, you are the unerring one," and "O Prajāpati. Thereafter he offers the *sauviṣṭakṛta* oblation with: "To Agni Kavyavāhana, the *sviṣṭakṛt*, *svadhā*! *Namaḥ* to the ancestors! *Svāhā*! (15)

On the following day, he immolates a cow for the ancestors. Having kindled the fire as before and performed an expiation with clarified butter, he dedicates the animal with a single blade of sacrificial grass and a single-pronged omentum-spit, saying: "I dedicate thee, acceptable to the ancestors. Thus he dedicates this cow to the ancestors, [saying]: "May the ancestors who have assembled accept her, who is full of vigor and full of milk."

"May she, rich in fat, rich in ghee, and rich in *svadhā*, satisfy my ancestors for the world beyond"—having thus offered the introductory oblation, he sprinkles the animal with the formula, "I sprinkle thee, acceptable to the ancestors," and they immolate it after it has been circumambulated by fire, its head turned westward and its feet toward the south. When it has been immolated, having replenished its vital breaths with water, he extracts the omentum silently and then removes the heart. Having roasted the omentum on a spit made of *udumbara* wood, he roasts the other organs separately on spits also made of *udumbara* wood, as previously determined.

Having cooked it, he offers the omentum—spread with clarified butter and sprinkled over—with a ladle made of *udumbara* wood, saying: "Carry the omentum, O Jātavedas, to the fathers where you know them to be placed in the distance; let streams of fat flow toward them; may their blessings be true according to their desires! Svadhā! Adoration to the fathers! Svāhā! (16)

When the food has been set out, having taken portions of the boiled rice and the meats together, he offers an oblation of that mixed with clarified butter, saying: "Behold the Ekāṣṭakā, yielding her milk—food rich in meat, rich in ghee, and rich in *svadhā*. May it be for me inexhaustible and imperishable, purified by the Brāhmaṇas. *Svadhā* and obeisance to the ancestors! *Svāhā!* The Ekāṣṭakā, performing penance as the consort of the year, yielded her milk while she was full."

Upon that milk may you subsist, O Fathers, as she is released in a thousand ways; from the east, svadhā! Adoration to the Fathers! Svāhā! O Jātavedas, carry the food to the Fathers wherever you know them to be placed in the distance.

"May streams of food flow toward them; may their blessings be realized according to their desires! *Svadhā*! *Namaḥ* to the ancestors! *Svāhā*!"—with these words he offers these additional oblations (*upahoma*) before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. "She who first shone forth, the *ekāṣṭakā*, performing penance; she who first shone forth, the image of the year, O Prajāpati"—with these five verses [he offers]. Then he offers the *sauviṣṭakṛta* oblation with: "To Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, *svadhā*! *Namaḥ* to the ancestors! *Svāhā*! On the following day...
He performs the monthly *śrāddha* for the ancestors with the remains of the meat, according to the procedure of the monthly *śrāddha*.

Having studied the Veda, he bathes and prepares the following items: a fuel-stick of *palāśa* wood, a water-pot, a mat of *eraka* grass, a pillow, a ball of bathing powder, sandalwood ground with all-fragrant substances, a cord with its case, a jewel with its loop, a bead of jujube wood, an upper garment, two ear-rings with their settings, a large and a small one, a wreath, collyrium, a mirror, sandals, a staff, and an umbrella. Then [he considers] the lunar mansions: Tiṣya, the two Uttaraphalgunīs, Hasta, Citrā, Svāti, and Viśākhā.

Thus, at one of these [times] before sunrise, he enters the cow-pen; for on this very day, he (the Sun) indeed burns with his heat over those who have bathed. Therefore, he should not let the sun scorch him on this day. Having closed the door with a skin with the hair side inward, and having established the fire in the eastern part of the pen, he places a fuel-stick of *palāśa* wood at midday, [saying]: "This hymn of praise we fashion with our inspired thought for the worthy Jātavedas, as one fashions a chariot."

"For auspicious is his providence in the assembly; O Agni, in your friendship may we not suffer harm—svāhā! Then, having brought all these materials at once, he places them to the north of the fire; then, having spread an eraka-grass mat to the north-west of the fire, behind the place for pouring water, he sits down upon it with his head toward the north. 18.

To the south, the barber sits down; he consecrates the barber’s razor with the mantra: "Auspicious is your name; the axe is your father; homage be to you; do not harm me. He consecrates it as it is being lifted up with water with the mantra: "Be auspicious to me when you touch. He consecrates the razor as it is being applied with the mantra: "The triple life-span of the seers, the triple life-span of Jamadagni and Kaśyapa..."

"Whatever triple life-span belongs to the gods, may that triple life-span be mine," [he says] as he shaves. "With the razor, well-fashioned and beautiful, which you, the shaver, shave with splendor—the face—do not steal away our life," [he says] after having the beard shaved; then he has the armpits shaved, then the hair, then the limbs starting from the feet. In this very same way he has himself shaved thereafter. Sitting in the western half of the cow-pen, having untied his girdle, he hands it to the attendant, saying, "Having taken this, hide it in a clump of grass. He, having taken it, hides it in a clump of grass.

"I embrace this one; I embrace the hating rival of such-and-such a son; he is superior to his enemies. Then the waters settle—both hot and cold; he pours the cold water into the hot for the sake of distinguishing between the divine and the human, so it is known. He sprinkles [the candidate] with mixed waters with the three verses beginning "O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss," with the four verses beginning "Golden-colored, bright, purifying," and with the entire section beginning "Pavamāna, who dwells in light," after having warmed him with bathing materials.

He cleanses his teeth for the sake of eating food, saying: "Arrange yourselves; Soma the King has come here. May he enter me with the enjoyment of food, and may I become long-lived and an eater of food. While being smeared with all-fragrant [ointment], he sprinkles himself, saying: "Homage to Śākajañjabha; homage to those deities who seize by force. Then he anoints himself, saying: "Whatever luster is in the Apasaras and whatever glory is in the Gandharvas..."

"May that divine and human fragrance enter me here"—having thus raised [the vessel], while being anointed with sandalwood, he sprinkles [him] in this manner and anoints him in this manner. Then he puts on a new inner garment with the formula, "Thou art life; may I attain old age. Having made the upper sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and having sipped water, he offers these oblations after having offered the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* formulas: "Dīkṣā, austerity, Mātariśvan, Bṛhaspati—these are the womb of this speech."

"May the Vedas and auspicious branches of knowledge abide in me; O Agni and Soma, bestow glory upon us! By that through which Agni shines, by that through which Soma shines, by that through which the Sun shines, by that through which Virāj shines—by that may I shine forth on every side here, becoming the sole sovereign. Svāhā! (20)

Sitting to the west of the fire facing east, he strings a bead from jujube wood (*bādara*) together with its cord and a supporting base. Having placed it in a vessel of water, he causes it to float around clockwise. [With the mantra: "O herb, thou art the protecting, the conquering, the powerful one; may she make me radiant with gold and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*). Having lifted it out and carried it around diagonally, he fastens it on. With the words, "Thou art without a noose," he places it upon his chest, saying: "Do not crush my chest; lie upon me auspiciously for my long life of a hundred autumns."

With his hand [he holds] a *bādara* (jujube) bead; the *mūrgasī* bead is for the Brāhmaṇa, the *pulaka* bead for the Vaiśya, and the *gardabhasugrīva* bead for the King. The *arka* bead is for the Brāhmaṇa, the *pulaka* bead for the Vaiśya, and the *gardabhasugrīva* bead for the King. For whichever [bead one chooses], there is a verse regarding the wearing of the bead: "The *kapitthaka* [bead]... Having placed it, he puts on an unwashed inner garment with the mantra, "For long life, thee! and the upper garment with, "May I attain old age! Having tied two loops in the fringe of the unwashed garment and placed them in a ladle, he offers an oblation of clarified butter, saying: "This [bead] bestows long life, splendor, great heroism, increase of wealth, and prosperity."
May gold enter me for long life, for splendor, and for victory— svāhā! [I offer] the high-spirited one, the conqueror of armies, the subduer of foes, the winner of wealth.
All prosperities and powers are contained within this gold; *svāhā*.
I have grasped the auspicious name of gold as that of a father; *svāhā*.
Make me, who possess the luster of gold, dear among men; *svāhā*.
Make me dear among the gods; make me dear among the brahmins;
make me dear among all the śūdras; make me dear among the kings, svāhā!
[May] Saṃrāj and Svarāj, and whatever blessings are in our home, [be ours].
"May we be united with that Fortune which is at the head of the kingdom; Svāhā!

(21) Having lifted it up and washed it, he first fastens it on the right side with the mantra, "Bestowing long life, bestowing luster. One should know that this same [formula] applies to the fastening of jeweled earrings. Then he fastens a garland.
O Śrūbhikā, ascend my head, beautifying my face;
indeed, beautify my face and increase my fortune.
"That which Jamadagni brought for Śraddhā, for desire, and for another—that very thing I now fasten on myself, together with fortune and splendor.
