Then he applies collyrium: "The collyrium from Trikakud, produced upon the Himavat, [I apply] as mountain-splendor within me. He gazes into a mirror: "Whatever splendor has departed from me while I was looking at my own self..."

With the mantra, "This, indeed, he takes up again with fortune and luster," he remains silent until the rising of the stars. When the stars have risen, he puts on his sandals with the mantra, "Thou art heaven" for the right one, and "Thou art earth" for the left one; having put them on, he consecrates them with the mantra, "Ye two are supports, O divine ones; do not cause me distress. He takes up his staff with the mantra, "For the world, for the Vedas, for the slaying of those who hate me, for my rivals, wild beasts, reptiles, and elephants. He takes up his umbrella with the mantra, "Thou art the refuge of Prajāpati, of Brahman..."

Having gone out with the verse, "The roof," he gazes at the quarters with the verse, "O six wide goddesses, make room for us. He gazes at the moon with the verse, "O King Soma, do not deliver me over to the hater who hates me. Having conversed with someone toward whom he has a friendly disposition, he goes about his business; this is one way. Now, another: having silently bathed at a sacred ford (tīrtha) and come out, he silently places a fuel-stick of *palāśa* wood on the fire. For a year he abstains from sexual intercourse, or for twelve nights, or for three nights; these are all the prescribed observances. 22.

Then, desiring to fetch the *arghya* water, he announces the *arghya*: "I wish to fetch it; do so! He brings curds into a bronze vessel (*kaṃsa*) and pours honey into it; having poured it into the smaller vessel, he covers it with the larger one. First, he approaches with the *kūrca* grass mat; following after him comes the water for washing the feet (*pādya*), then the *arghya*, then the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and finally the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*). Then he announces a seat to him; he responds to that with the mantra: "Thou art the sustainer of the kingdom, the teacher’s seat; may I not abandon thee! This applies whether he is a king or a Brahmin.

"Thou art the sustainer of the kingdom, the throne of sovereignty; may I not be separated from thee," [with these words] the village headman or the army commander [approaches]. Then he causes water for washing the feet to be announced to him, and he responds with this mantra: "May the waters that wash the feet destroy my enemy. May I be endowed with Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcasa*) in this family; may greatness be in me, glory in me, and sensory power and vigor in me.

May glory and splendor come to me; unite me with milk and brilliance. Make me dear to all creatures and the lord of cattle. Having received the left foot, he should receive the right foot—the king, the village headman, or the army commander [receiving it first]. (23)

Then, when it is announced to him, "The guest-water (arghya)," he responds with this very formula: "Thou art the milking of Virāj; may I obtain the milking of Virāj; may the milking of the Padyā Virāj be in me. Having accepted it, he pours it out [with the verse]: "I send you forth to the ocean; go back to your own source."

"May I be without flaw in my progeny; may you not spill me away, O milk! O milk!"—having said this, they announce, "Water for sipping. He sips it with the formula: "Thou art the under-layer for the nectar. When he has sipped the water, they announce, "The honey-mixture (madhuparka). He addresses that with the mantra: "By that which is the honeyed, supreme form of honey, the essence of food, by that honeyed, supreme form of honey, the essence of food, may I become the supreme eater of food, honeyed. Having accepted it, he consumes it for the sake of the threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*).

"You are glory, the glory of glory; you are the radiance of Brahman. Make me dear to all creatures, the lord of cattle. Having sipped water three times with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he then gives it to the guest for consumption, or he himself consumes it all. Then he has water brought to him for rinsing the mouth; having rinsed his mouth with "Thou art the covering of immortality," he is then informed that a cow is ready for him. He addresses her with the mantra: "Thou art a cow; thou art one whose evil is struck away. Strike away evil! Strike away the evil of both myself and so-and-so. Slay my enemy; make my enemy perish! 24.

Then, having prepared food for him and announced that it is ready, he says, "Feed four Brāhmaṇas of different lineages. When they have eaten, they bring food [for him]. Having addressed it with this same mantra, accepted it, and descended from his seat, he eats it. One view is that he should eat the foods after descending from his seat, just as he did with the *madhuparka*. Now, there is this other view: this rule applies only to those who are worthy of honor (*arha*); regarding others, he may act according to his desire. Furthermore, if he releases a cow, he addresses her with a mantra.

The cow is worthy of being a milch-cow; she is the mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Ādityas, and the navel of immortality. Let me speak forth to the discerning person: do not slay the cow, the Aditi! Let her drink water and eat grass.

"Oṃ, release! Then, having made the sacrificial cord (yajñopavīta) over the left shoulder for the Soma-proclaimer (*somapravāka*), and having sipped water, standing or sitting facing east or north, he mutters: "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! You have proclaimed long life for me; you have proclaimed luster for me; you have proclaimed glory for me; you have proclaimed prosperity for me. May I become long-lived, lustrous, glorious, prosperous, and honored. Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! May I become everything. Having said this, he responds to the speech with the formula ending in "May that not fail me," using the same [formula] for the Bhūta-proclaimer (*bhūtapravāka*). 25.

Then, having obtained food for him, he consecrates it with the mantra: "May I be like food to your sight; may I be like wealth to your sight. You are prosperity; enter us from this side. Let the great quarters flow together; let pleasant truths come together. May all desires come toward me; may my dear ones protect me. You are glory; may I be glorious in you, O [Name]! Having thus consecrated it, one who wishes to engage in trade, taking a portion of the merchandise, offers it while saying: "O gods, as I move about in commerce with wealth, desiring wealth with wealth."

"May Soma bestow radiance upon him; may Agni, Īśāna, Indra, and Bṛhaspati [bestow it], svāhā! Then, for the purpose of winning a dispute, when he is about to enter a debate, having covered his head with his upper garment and held the umbrella with his left hand, he offers a handful of chaff with his right hand, saying: "O Avajihvaka, O Nijihvaka, I worship you with an oblation! That which I speak is the truth; may that other person speak lower than me, svāhā! He then addresses the one with whom he is debating: "I take your speech from your mouth, from your mind, and from your heart."

"From limb to limb I take away your speech; wherever your speech was deposited, that I take from you. That which I speak is the truth: 'Fall down lower than me! [26] If his good servants should run away, he should kindle the fire and offer oblations with the *iṣṭakā* verses: 'The day has followed after you; the night has followed after you. He has turned you back; he has made you turn back. May Indra’s cry of reproach cry out against you on every side, if you have despised me, O non-gods, as one who is more godlike than a god.'"

"May Indra, having bound you with a noose, bring you back to me again," he should say; or, having driven in a stake made of *khadira* wood, he should wrap it three times counter-clockwise with two threads—one blue and one red—saying, "O turner, turn [them] back! Indeed, even if they have gone far away, they will surely turn back here. If he should desire of someone, "May this person not escape from me," he should seize that person by the right hand, [reciting]: "In whom the past and the future, and all the gods are gathered together."

With the words, "Therefore I take hold of you; I take hold of you for myself; I take hold of you for Brahman," he does not indeed fall away from him whom he should desire, thinking, "May this man not be severed from me. On the night of the new moon, while [the victim] is sleeping, having brought his own urine into a living-horn vessel, he should walk around him three times, sprinkling it with his right hand turned away (apassavya), saying: "I have taken hold of you from the mountain, from your brother, from your sister, and from all your kinsmen. You are seized and hated. Constantly pursued by a furious pursuer, may you be cut off!"

"You are sprinkled around with urine; you are sprinkled around with urine"—thus [he says], for one who is about to sit for a long sacrificial session (*dīrghasattra*) does not indeed fall away from this [state]. 27.

One who is about to go on a journey entrusts his wife with a protective charm (*paridā*). Having had coarse *āḍhārikā* seeds ground into powder, he scatters it over her private parts while she is asleep on the night of the new moon, saying: "O Soma, protect her from other men; let there be no *mad* [intoxication] for others. Even if many desire her on that night, they certainly do not succeed. If he should wish, "May they succeed," he should say to her: "Wash your sides with the urine of a brown dog. When about to go on a journey, he addresses her: "We shall dwell here; we shall dwell in breath, in life."

Then he addresses him with this mantra: "Come hither, O Indra, with your pleasant, peacock-haired bay horses. Let no one, not even those with snares, restrain you. Go as if along a path already trodden. O Prāṇa, dwell in the life-span of that person; be established in the earth, in Agni; in Vāyu, in the intermediate space, in Sūrya, and in heaven. That well-being which Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, Candramas, and the Waters follow—follow that well-being, O [Name]!"

Having begun with "Descend, O Lord of the World," and ending with "Having become a hawk, fly away," he should look upon one whom he desires with this triplet of verses, [thinking] "May he return safely. He returns right here. If he should desire, "May he not return," he should look upon him with the verse, "Fly away, O consumption! Then he addresses him with the mantra: "May Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, lead you to the furthest distance, from which you shall not return for eternal years. He indeed does not return. 28

Now, regarding the mounting of the chariot: if he obtains a chariot, he should have it yoked during the waxing fortnight under an auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). When about to mount, he touches the two side-pieces (*pakṣasī*) with the words, "Thou art the *Bṛhat*," the right one; "Thou art the *Rathaṃtara*," the left one; and "Thou art the *Vāmadevya*," the middle one. Having mounted the horse, he wipes the two wheels with the remainder of the section beginning, "The two *Aṅkas*, the two *Nyaṅkas* on both sides. If it is a peaceful chariot (*śamaratha*), then having placed the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) over his shoulder, sipped water, and touched the ground, he recites: "Here is support, here is self-support, here is delight, here..."

"Ramatī" [is the mantra]. Now, regarding the mounting of an elephant: if he obtains an elephant, having prepared it during the waxing moon under an auspicious lunar mansion, he mounts it, saying: "This one, the son of such-and-such a person, I pierce with the thunderbolt of Indra; may I be superior to my enemies. Then he causes it to walk forward, saying: "Carry on, O Time; carry on, O Fortune; bring fortune to me. This is the same as with the peaceful chariot. If he should mount upon a bare piece of ground that has not been strewn, he consecrates it with: "Homage to Rudra who dwells on the earth, who has the wind as his arrow; homage to Rudra!"

With the formula, "Homage to Rudra who dwells on the earth," he releases [the cow] during the *sarpasṛt* (serpent-path); with the formula, "Homage to Rudra who moves through the serpent-path, whose arrow is the wind; homage to Rudra; homage to Rudra who moves through the serpent-path," he mutters during the *śakṛtsṛt* (dung-path); with the formula, "Homage to Rudra who dwells in the dung, whose arrow is the wind; homage to Rudra; homage to Rudra who dwells in the dung," [he acts]. If fresh cow-dung lies across his path, he should cross over it after saying, "Thou art the cow-pen. 29.

If he should pass by a crossroads, he consecrates it with this mantra: "Homage to Rudra who dwells on the earth, whose arrow is the wind; homage to Rudra! Homage to Rudra who dwells on the earth! If he should pass by a cemetery, he consecrates it with this mantra: "Homage to Rudra who dwells there, whose arrow is the wind; homage to Rudra! Homage to Rudra who dwells there! Upon seeing a river containing crocodiles, he mutters: "Homage to Rudra who dwells in the waters, whose arrow is the wind; homage to Rudra! Homage to Rudra who dwells in the waters! If a whirlwind should strike him...

If it should come near, he consecrates it with: "Homage to Rudra who dwells in the intermediate space, whose arrow is the wind; homage to Rudra! Homage to Rudra who dwells in the intermediate space! If a shower of rain should fall upon him, he consecrates it with: "Thou art a shower, yet thou art not a shower; thou art a thunderbolt; homage be to thee; do not harm me. If a bird should alight upon him, he consecrates it with: "Those birds that spread their wings, fearing destruction along with [the powers of] misfortune..."

"May they sprinkle me with auspicious and sharp splendor and vigor"—with these words he should sprinkle him with water. If a fruit should fall upon him, he consecrates it with the mantra: "If a fruit has fallen from a tree, or if from the atmosphere, that is indeed Vāyu."

If it rains upon him while he is drenched during a drought, he sprinkles himself with water, reciting: "Wherever the waters touched his body or his garment, may they drive away Destruction (Nirṛti) far away. He then consecrates that [rain] with the mantra: "From the great heaven, from the mid-air, a drop of water has fallen upon me with auspiciousness; with my senses and mind I have come hither, fashioned by the sacred word (Brahman) and by good deeds. Thus he should sprinkle himself with water. 30.

Having seen a variegated tree, he murmurs: "May fire burn far from you; may the axe be far from you. May rain shower upon you where there is no wind; live for a thousand years! Homage be to you, O tree; may it be well with me, O tree! Before midday, he should daily touch trees that yield milky sap, and the *nyagrodha* tree everywhere. When the fire has spontaneously ignited itself, he should place two pieces of fuel upon it, [murmuring]: "Shine forth, O Jātavedas, driving away destruction from me."

"Bring cattle to me and bestow life from every direction, Svāhā! Do not harm us, O Jātavedas—neither cow, horse, nor human being. Without causing injury, O Agni, come hither; protect prosperity within me, Svāhā! Having established [the fire] with these words, he stands in attendance, reciting: "Homage to Rudra who sits in the fire, whose arrows are the winds; homage to Rudra, homage to Rudra who sits in the fire. Whatever misfortune, defeat, slander, or sneezing, whatever bad dream or ill-omened cry from birds—this I direct against my enemies.

"Whatever has been experienced as ill-omened by birds, or whatever was traversed by a deer across [one's path], that I entrust to my enemies. May the evil omen go far away; may the sneeze go far away. Let the twitching of the eye, the bad dream, and the unsuccessful sacrifice reach him who hates us. He mutters this mantra during a physical affliction or an injury, according to the specific signs. In every such case, he should touch water. 31

Now, these are the expiations for portents: if a dove alights upon the sacrificial post, if honey is found in the house, if a pillar has sprouted, or if an anthill rises up; having fasted for a day, wearing clean clothes, and having conversed with a Brāhmaṇa, when the sun has set, he should kindle the fire within the inner chamber, offer the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations, and then offer these following oblations: *pūrṇā darvi parā pata*, *imaṃ me varuṇa*, *tattvā yāmi*, *tvaṃ no agne*, *sa tvaṃ no agne*, and *tvamagne*.

"O Agni, drive away curses and misfortunes; whatever I have done in excess of this rite, O Prajāpati,"—having offered the final oblation with these words, he should serve food to the Brāhmaṇas. Then, in milk, there is a *sthālīpāka* (cooked offering) which is conducive to progeny, cattle, heaven, long life, and self-sustenance; with that he should sacrifice. At all the festival-occasions (*parvan*), having placed fuel of *udumbara* wood upon the fire, he offers the *sthālīpāka*—previously spread with clarified butter and subsequently sprinkled over—with a ladle made of *udumbara* wood, reciting: "May a thousand come first to the brown one, together with glory."

May Babhru, the tawny-eyed one, having arrived with his thousandfold host, desire [this for me], Svāhā! O Jātavedas, bring life to me from every direction; so that I may dwell in the favor of the multiformed cattle, Svāhā! The essence gathered from the gods, the great glory belonging to Prajāpati—the essence of foods I offer; may my fame be flawless, Svāhā! Agni moves within Agni, having entered it; he is the son of the Ṛṣis, this sovereign king.

"Having consecrated with the *svāhā* call, I offer this to you with the *brahman*; may I not wrongly deprive the gods of their portion. May our portion not be confounded; *svāhā*! Thus, according to the instruction, are the optional offerings and the *bali* oblations. 32. Thus ends the second book in the *Bhāradvāja-sūtra*.

If the single sacred fire (*ekāgni*) has been interrupted for twelve days, it must be re-established; this is the fire pertaining to the initiation (*aupanāyanika*), the tending of which with fuel-sticks during the period of studentship is prescribed for morning and evening according to the instruction. One who has completed his bath (*snāta*) should tend it with herbs or with whatever food is available. Likewise, when her husband has died, a woman should do so from the time of marriage onwards. The *pārvaṇa* sacrifice should be performed on the full moon or new moon day, or under the asterisms of Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, or the two Punarvasus. Having dug up the ground, sprinkled it with water, strewn it with sand, and enclosed it with a fence, one should establish the fire at midday.

Having churned fire from sacrificial wood or having brought ordinary fire, he places it down with the *praṇava*. The Brahman priest impels [the sacrificer] with the *praṇava*. Seated, [the Adhvaryu] lays the fire down with the *vyāhṛtis* and the *praṇava*: "Bhūḥ bhuvaḥ suvaḥ oṃ! I place you, O Agni, upon the earth, in immortality; I place you in truth, in immortality; I place you in Ṛta, in immortality; I place you in the Immortal, setting aside evil deeds and [establishing] good deeds. Then, with these [formulas]: "Upon the earth, I place you in immortality; I place you in truth, in immortality; I place you in Ṛta, in immortality..."

"I place you in immortality; I place you in immortality"—with these words, he pacifies [the fire] with clarified butter, with herbs, and with three pacifying oblations: "O Agni, that form of yours which is purifying (*pavamānā*), which is dear among cattle, which is on the earth, which is in the fire, which is in the *Rathantara* [Sāman], and which is in the *Gāyatrī* metre—this I win for you from it; *svāhā* to it! O Agni, that form of yours which is purifying (*pāvakā*), which is dear in the waters, which is in the intermediate space, which is in the wind, which is in the *Vāmadevya* [Sāman], and which is in the *Triṣṭubh* metre—this I win for you from it; *svāhā* to it!"

"O Agni, that pure and beloved body of yours which is in the sun, which is in heaven, in the Āditya, in the Bṛhat, and in the Jāgata metre—this [offering] of mine wins it for you; to that body of yours, Svāhā! With these words, he places three fuel-sticks of *aśvattha* wood, anointed with clarified butter, while reciting three verses beginning with "O Agni, you purify the lives. Then, with three verses beginning with "From the ocean the honeyed wave has risen," he places three sticks of *śamī* wood. With the verse "O Agni, kindled, shine before us," he places a stick of *udumbara* wood. And with the verse "We would worship you in your highest birth, O Agni," he places a stick of *vikaṅkata* wood. That [is the procedure].

Having offered a fuel-stick made of *śamī* wood into the *aupāsana* fire silently with the verse "citrāṃ devānām" (RV 4.1.3), and having worshipped it with the two sections beginning with "yāste agne ghorāstanuvaḥ" (TS 3.4.11) and "snik ca snīhitiśca" (TS 3.4.11), the ritual procedure for the *dārvihoma* is the same; having performed the ritual procedure for the *dārvihoma*, [he concludes]. 1.

Having placed clarified butter on the fire and purified it, and having heated and wiped both the *sruva* and the *juhū* ladles, he fills the *sruk* with four portions or twelve portions of butter and offers the full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), reciting the verse, "Seven are thy kindling-sticks, O Agni, seven thy tongues," and concluding with the exclamation *svāhā*. When the full-oblation has been offered, he gives a boon: either a cow, a garment, a draft-ox, or gold. Having taken four portions of butter into the *sruk*, he offers three *tantumatī* oblations, beginning with, "Stretching the thread, wake up, O Agni."

Having taken another fourfold portion with the formula, "Thirty-three threads," he offers four *abhyāvartinī* oblations with the verses, "O Agni, thou who turnest back," and "O Agni Aṅgiras, return with vigor and wealth. Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers the *anukhyā* oblation with the verse, "Agni has looked along the forefront of the dawns. Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers with the *manasvatī* verse, "May the mind, the light, enjoy [the offering]. Having taken another fourfold portion, he offers the *prājāpatyā* oblation with the formula, "To Prajāpati. Another...

Having taken four portions, he offers with the *vyāhṛtis* one by one and also with them all together; some say he should offer each four-portioned ladle individually, while others say it is according to what has been prescribed. In all *darvihoma* offerings, one may act as one pleases. Having offered the *jayas*, the *abhyātānas*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*, [he proceeds].

Having cooked rice in this very fire, he offers four oblations of food, saying: "To Agni, svāhā! To Agni Pavamāna, svāhā! To Agni Pāvaka, svāhā! To Agni Śuci, svāhā! And with every new crop, he offers to these deities of the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice—with Sviṣṭakṛt as the fourth, or with Sviṣṭakṛt as the fifth—saying: "To Indra and Agni, svāhā! To the Viśve Devas, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā! To Heaven and Earth, svāhā! To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā!"

Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he performs five supplementary oblations (*upahoma*) with the mantra, "To him who has a hundred weapons, who has a hundred powers... and so forth. Then he should feed Brāhmaṇas. For as long as he lives, he attends to this fire every evening and morning with rice or barley. At evening, he offers the first oblation with "Svāhā to Agni," and the second with "Svāhā to Prajāpati. In the morning, he offers [the first] with "Svāhā to Sūrya" and the second with "Svāhā to Prajāpati. Now, if he should wish to depart on a journey, the procedure for living abroad (*pravasatha-kalpa*) has already been explained.

The placing of the fuel-stick (*samitsamāropaṇa*) and the descent [of the fire] (*upāvarohaṇa*)—some authorities prescribe the placing of the fuel-stick either upon oneself or in the two kindling woods (*araṇī*); and the descent is explained as being performed in the common fire. Thus concludes the rule for the single fire; thus concludes the ritual procedure for the *aupāsana* fire. 3.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the initiation and dismissal of the vows. On a festival day during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, from the kindling of the fire up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, one offers oblations with the formulas: "To the Hotṛs, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! To the Viśvedevas, svāhā! To the Self-existent One, svāhā!"—thus for the Hotṛs; and for the Upaniṣads: "To the Sāṃhitī deities of the Upaniṣads, svāhā! To the Vāruṇī deities of the Upaniṣads, svāhā! To all the deities of the Upaniṣads, svāhā!"—thus for the Upaniṣads.

He places four fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood, anointed with clarified butter, or from any one of the sacrificial trees, [with the formula]: "O Agni, Lord of Vows, for the sake of the Hotṛs I shall perform the vow; may I be able to do so, may it be successful for me, svāhā!"

"O Vāyu, Lord of Vows! O Āditya, Lord of Vows! O Lord of Vows of vows! I shall perform the vow for the sake of the Hotṛ-priests; may I be able to do it; may it be successful for me, Svāhā!"—thus [he says]. "I shall perform the vow for the sake of the Upaniṣads; may I be able to do it; may it be successful for me, Svāhā!"—thus [he says]. "Mind and Intelligence"—with these words he proceeds to the Jaya-offerings and so forth. Having performed the rites up to the sprinkling around, he then instructs him: "You are a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī); place fuel on the fire; drink water; perform your duties; do not sleep during the day; go on your alms-round; remain dependent upon your teacher; study the Veda. 4.

For forty-eight years, or twenty-four years, or indeed for all his life, or for a minimum of twelve years from the time of initiation—alternatively, it is said that he should observe this vow for one year; when that year has elapsed, from the kindling of the fire up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, he offers two *mindā* oblations with the verses, "Whatever deficiency has occurred in my self" and "Agni has given back my sight," as before. Having offered the principal oblations, he causes the vows to be undertaken for the lords of vows (*vratapati*) with the formula: "O Agni, lord of vows, I have performed the vow for the Hotṛs."

"May that be accomplished for me; may it be successful for me, svāhā! O Vāyu, Lord of Vows! O Āditya, Lord of Vows! O Lord of Vows among vows! I have performed the vow before the Hotṛs; may that be accomplished for me; may it be successful for me, svāhā! "I have performed the vow before the Upaniṣads; may that be accomplished for me; may it be successful for me, svāhā! With the words "Thought and Thinking," he proceeds with the *jayas* and so forth, performing the rites up to the final sprinkling (*pariṣecana*). Then, at the conclusion of the vow, he causes him to study or causes him to hear [the texts], saying, "The Great Hotṛs, the Upaniṣads. Thus concludes the instruction and dismissal of the vow; thus concludes the instruction and dismissal of the vow. 5.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*). On a festival day during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious constellation, in the afternoon, having shaved his hair and beard, and having gone out toward the east or the north, he establishes the fire on a barren spot where no roof is visible, spreads grass around it, performs the introductory rite as before, touches the *madantī* water, and having performed the pacification with the first *anuvāka*, he places four fuel sticks of *udumbara* wood, anointed with clarified butter, with the mantras beginning "The earth is the fuel-stick. Then...

The deity attends upon him: "O Agni, Lord of Vows, I shall perform the Śukriya vow; may I be able to do so, may it be successful for me. O Vāyu, Lord of Vows; O Āditya, Lord of Vows; O Lord of Vows among vows, I shall perform the Śukriya vow; may I be able to do so, may it be successful for me. Then he causes him to recite the beginnings of all the sections (anuvākas), or he begins with the *jayas* and so forth of the first and last sections. Having performed the rites ending with the sprinkling of water, and having touched the boiling water (*madantī*), he performs the propitiation (*śānti*) with the final section.

Having done this, he then causes [the child] to close its eyes and restrains its speech; then, with an unwashed garment, he wraps its head from the front. When the sun has set, he brings it into the village. Remaining silent that night, he either stands or sits. On the following day, having established the fire in a cleared spot where the roof-rafters are not visible and having strewn grass around it, he then shows him six or seven things—some say seven: the fire, the sun, a water-pot, a stone, a calf, a Mahānagnī woman, and gold as the seventh.

He shows him the three musical instruments; then he worships the sun with the verse, "The birds, the fair-winged. At this point, having given the garment to the teacher, he undertakes his lifelong studentship (*brahmacarya*). He should not eat at night; if he should eat, he should eat only what is well-kindled by fire. He should not drink from an earthen vessel. He should not converse with a woman or a *śūdra*. He should not mount a vehicle with wheels, nor descend into a well. He should not wear shoes, nor carry an umbrella. He should not look upon an assembly, nor palaces, nor [decorated] bodies, nor a corpse, nor an outcaste (*antāvasāyin*). 6.

He shall observe this vow for one year. When the year has elapsed, at a time when the ground is uncultivated and no roof-covering is visible, he should perform the rites from the kindling of the fire up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings. Having offered two *mindāhuti* oblations, he should offer the principal oblations as before. After touching the warm water (*madantī*), having performed the pacification (*śānti*) with the first *anuvāka*, and having placed four fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood with the mantras beginning "The earth is even" (*pṛthivī samit*), he worships the deities with those same mantras repeated. Then he causes [the student] to recite the beginnings of all the *anuvākas*.

Or, having performed the *śānti* rite with the first or the last [verse], he proceeds to the *jaya* and other rites; having completed everything up to the *pariṣecana*, he then instructs him, beginning with "Thou art a student of sacred knowledge" (*brahmacāry asi*) and ending with "one who dwells at the end" (*antāvasāyī*), the instruction being as before. 7.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the commencement and the dismissal [of Vedic study]. During the fortnight of the Śravaṇā constellation, when the herbs have grown, or on the full moon day of the month of Hasta, one performs the *upākarma* (commencement of study). From the kindling of the fire up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, one makes oblations to the *kāṇḍarṣis* (the seers of the sections) or to the names of the sections. For those texts belonging to Prajāpati, he offers with "To Prajāpati, the seer of the section, svāhā! or simply "To Prajāpati, svāhā!"; for those belonging to Soma, with "To Soma, the seer of the section, svāhā! or "To Soma, svāhā!"; for those belonging to Agni, with "To Agni, the seer of the section, svāhā! or "To Agni, svāhā!"; and for those belonging to the Viśvedevas...

With the formula "Svāhā to the gods, the Ṛṣis of the sections," he offers the Vaiśvadeva oblations; or with "Svāhā to the Viśve Devas," or "Svāhā to the Self-existent. Sadasaspati is the second [deity] for all. They study the first three Anuvākas, or the beginnings of the Kāṇḍas, or the whole [text]. He may suspend his studies for three days or one day. Then he should study again. He should not study during the month of Prauṣṭhapada, nor at nightfall. The suspension of study (utsarga) takes place under the constellation Rohiṇī in the fortnight following the full moon of Taiṣa, or on the full moon of Māgha. Together with his pupils, having gone out toward the east or the north to where there is water, [he performs the rite].

Having gone there to waters that are easy to enter, not turbid, and full of shells, and having performed the ritual purification (*mārjana*) with the three verses beginning "O Waters, you who are sources of bliss" (*apo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*), with the four verses beginning "Gold-colored, pure, purifying" (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*), and with this entire section (*anuvāka*) beginning "Pavamāna, [dwelling] in the world of light" (*pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*), they should hold three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn: "From the kindled heat, Right (*ṛta*) and Truth (*satya*) were born;
from that, the night was born; from that, the ocean and the billowing sea."
From the ocean, the vast sea, the year was born;
ordaining days and nights, the Lord of all that blinks, the Ordainer fashioned the sun and the moon according to the ancient order.

Having handed over darbha grass to one another, saying, "Heaven and earth, the intermediate space, and then the sun," they prepare seats for Brahmā, Prajāpati, Agni, Bṛhaspati, Vāyu, Sūrya, Candramas, the Nakṣatras, Indra the king, Soma the king, Yama the king, Varuṇa the king, Vaiśravaṇa the king, Rudra, Skanda, Viṣṇu, the two Aśvins, Dhanvantari, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, the Ṛbhus, and the Bhṛgus.
"To the Maruts, to the Atharvans, to the Aṅgirases"—thus for the *gaṇas*.

"To Viśvāmitra, to Jamadagni, to Bharadvāja, to Gautama, to Atri, to Vasiṣṭha, to Kaśyapa, to Arundhatī—I prepare [the seat]," thus on the south. To Agastya they prepare [the seat] on the north: "To Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, to Jātūkarṇa, to Tarukṣa, to Bṛhaduktha, to Tṛṇabindu, to Somaśravas, to Somaśuṣmin, to Vājaśravas, to Vājaratna, to Varmin, to Varūthin, to Satvavat, to Haryaśva, to Vāmadeva, to Udamaya, to Ṛṇañjaya, to Ṛtañjaya, to Kṛtañjaya."

"I offer this portion for Dhanañjaya, Babhru, Tryaruṇa, Trivarṣa, Tridhātu, Aśvayajña, Parāśara, Vasiṣṭha, Indra, Mṛtyu, Karta, Tvaṣṭṛ, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Savitṛ, Suśravas, Satyaśravas, Sāvitrī, the Metres, the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvāṅgirases, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, the Serpents and Divine Beings, and to all living beings. 10.

To the south, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he prepares portions for Vaiśampāyana Phaliṅgu, Tittiri Ukha, Ātreya the author of the *Pada-pāṭha*, Kauṇḍinya the author of the *Vṛtti*, Kaṇva, Bodhāyana, Bharadvāja the author of the *Sūtras*, Āpastamba, and all the authors of *Sūtras*, teachers, seers, forest-dwellers, those who have sublimated their vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*), and women devoted to a single husband, saying, "I prepare [this]"; and they likewise prepare portions separately for their own paternal ancestors and maternal ancestors by means of these very same [names].

With names, and with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food, fruits, and water—saying "Salutation to such-and-such! Salutation to such-and-such! with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps; saying "Svāhā to such-and-such! Svāhā to such-and-such! with food; and saying "I satiate such-and-such! I satiate such-and-such! with fruits and water—they pay homage here. They recite the first three *anuvākas* or all the *kāṇḍa*-openings, beginning with the verse, "From every joint it sprouts. Then, at the edge of the water, they plant *dūrvā* grass with two verses; then they make a pool with the verse, "Make the earth swell," using their hand.

Having thrice pierced the *tamitorāji* [the line of darkness], they run toward the *pārāyaṇa*; thus, at the conclusion of the *pārāyaṇa*, having studied the *an-aśnat-pārāyaṇa*, they perform this [rite] at the edge of water, excluding the planting of *dūrvā* grass and the running with curds. Having returned home, one should feed the Brahmins with cakes (*apūpa*), parched grains (*dhānā*), flour-meal (*saktu*), and boiled rice (*odana*). In this very same manner, one should daily satisfy the gods, the seers (*ṛṣi*), and the ancestors with water; one should satisfy them. 11.

In all *pākayajñas*, there is no *bali-mantra* for a woman or for one who has not been initiated (*anupeta*). Alternatively, a woman may offer the oblation, excluding the mantra; likewise, one who is uninitiated may do so. One who is initiated is explained by the rules for a householder. Regarding the offerings of food intended for sacrifice and *balis* which are connected with heaven and prosperity: when employing these mantras, one must sleep on the ground for twelve days, observe celibacy, and avoid pungent and salty foods; for the highest grade of rite, there is a fast for one night. A woman should perform the *vaiśvadeva* offering, or she may perform it herself if she is married; [the formula is] "devasya tvā..."

"By the impulse of Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I offer what is pleasing to the Viśve Devas"—with this *yajus* he offers three times, and the fourth time silently. The wife, being restrained, threshes the grain; [the husband] instructs the wife. After she has washed her hands and feet, he should place the pot on the fire. When it is cooked, he should announce it; she announces to her husband, "It is ready. He replies, "May that well-cooked food, the Virāj, not fail me! Having sprinkled it with clarified butter and removed it from the fire, he sets it down.

Having sprinkled clarified butter over the established [oblation], having sprinkled it with water from above and smeared it with cow-dung from below—here there is no fuel or sacrificial grass, nor are there the two *āghāra* libations or the two *ājyabhāga* portions; having placed four fuel-sticks with the *vyāhṛtis* and having sprinkled water around [the fire], he offers with his hand: "Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Soma! Svāhā to Prajāpati! Svāhā to Dhanvantari! Svāhā to Dhruva! Svāhā to Dhruva-Bhauma! Svāhā to Dhruvakṣiti! Svāhā to Acyutakṣiti! Svāhā to the Viśvedevas! Svāhā to all [beings]!"

He offers oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* one by one and also collectively: "To the deities, svāhā! To Agni, svāhā! To Agni Amavān, svāhā! To Agni Annāda, svāhā! To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā! [Then he recites: "Do not harm us in our children or grandchildren, nor in our life, nor in our cows, nor in our horses; do not strike down our heroes in your wrath, O Rudra. Bearing oblations, we worship you with reverence, svāhā! To desire, svāhā! To anger, svāhā! Then he sprinkles water around [the fire] and modifies the mantras accordingly. 12

Having wiped the fire with his hand from the other side, he offers: "To Dharma, svāhā! To Adharma, svāhā! To Dhruva, svāhā! To Kṣaya, svāhā! Then, [he offers] food: "To Prāṇa Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin, svāhā! into the *ukhā* pan; "To the Waters, svāhā! To Varuṇa, svāhā! into the *udadhānī*; "To Rudrāṇī, svāhā! To Rudra, svāhā! into the *rudrāṇī* pan; "Bhūḥ svāhā! to all the deities; "To the Atmosphere, svāhā! To the Plants and Forest Trees, svāhā! in the middle of the house; and "To Kāma, svāhā! in the place of the bed, [and] "To the Forest Trees."

"Svāhā! at the site of the pillar; "Svāhā to the herbs and trees! at the two pillars of the gate; "Svāhā to the householders, svāhā to the masters of the house, svāhā to the dwellings, svāhā to the masters of the dwellings, svāhā! in the north-eastern region; "Svāhā to the beings! at the opening; "Svāhā to that which moves, that which walks, and that which stirs—the portion of the Name, to the Name, svāhā! on the threshold; then on the lintel, "Svāhā to the Maruts," and in the middle, "Svāhā to Dhātṛ, svāhā to Vidhātṛ."

Having gone out from the house along two paths, he offers: "To the Day, svāhā! To the Night, svāhā! Then, upon reaching [the threshing floor], he offers: "To Piṅkṣāṇī, svāhā! To Piṅkṣāṇī, svāhā! Upon the Piṅkṣāṇī [stone], he offers: "To Viṣṇu, svāhā! To Viṣṇu, svāhā! On the mortar and pestle, he offers: "To Anas, svāhā! On the cart, he offers: "To Soma, svāhā! On the grain, he offers: "To Śrī, svāhā! To Puṣṭi, svāhā! On the heap of grain, he then pours out the oblation (bali) clockwise: "To the eastern quarter, svāhā! To the southern quarter, svāhā! To the western quarter, svāhā! To the northern quarter, svāhā!"

"Svāhā to the upward direction! Svāhā to the southeastern direction! Svāhā to the southwestern direction! Svāhā to the northwestern direction! Svāhā to the northeastern direction! Svāhā to Brahman! Svāhā to Prajāpati!"—thus in the center. 13.

"To Indra, Svāhā! To the attendants of Indra, Svāhā!"—thus in the east; "To Yama, Svāhā! To the attendants of Yama, Svāhā!"—thus in the south; "To Varuṇa, Svāhā! To the attendants of Varuṇa, Svāhā!"—thus in the west; "To Soma, Svāhā! To the attendants of Soma, Svāhā!"—thus in the north. Then, [he offers] "To Agni, Svāhā" in the east; "To Yama, Svāhā" in the south; "To Varuṇa, Svāhā" in the west; "To Soma, Svāhā" in the north; "To the Seven Seers, Svāhā! To all beings, Svāhā! in the northeast direction. Now...

To the south, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he offers oblations, saying: "Svadhā! Adoration to the fathers; svadhā! Adoration to the grandfathers; svadhā! Adoration to the great-grandfathers; svadhā! Adoration to the maternal grandfathers; svadhā! Adoration to the maternal great-grandfathers; svadhā! Adoration to the maternal great-great-grandfathers. Having touched water in the middle, he says, "Svadhā! Adoration to the descendants," and offers three [oblations]. Then, to the north, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), he offers oblations, saying: "Svāhā! To the Ṛgveda; svāhā! To the Yajurveda; svāhā! To the Sāmaveda; svāhā! To the Atharvaveda."

" Svāhā to the Atharvans and Aṅgirases! Svāhā to the Itihāsas and Purāṇas! Svāhā to all the divine beings! Svāhā to all creatures! Svāhā! Then he pours out the offering upward [with the words]: "Those beings who roam about by day, seeking the offering, the servants of Vituda—"

"Desiring nourishment, I offer this oblation to them; may the Lord of Nourishment bestow nourishment upon me, svāhā! Thus, at night, he offers the oblation with the verse beginning "Those who desire the oblation. Then, with a single leaf of the *arka* plant, he pours out the oblation with the verse: "To those whose mother does not cook, to those who gather at night—to those beings I shall give this ball of food unasked. May there be safety for me in fear, and abundance in times of famine."

At the time of the birth-slaughter—when death and birth prevail—he pours out the rinsing water of the vessels with the formula, "To Kāla, svāhā! At night, he pours it out for those who have taken refuge with the formula, "To Rudra, svāhā! Having performed the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, he should wait for a guest; or, having set aside the first portion until the time for milking the cows has passed, he should place it down, for this fifth sacrifice is indeed the guest (14).

Having sat down to the west of the *gārhapatya* fire and said, "Recite, sir," he should repeat the *Sāvitrī* one thousand times or one hundred times; he should mutter the beginnings of the Vedas ten times and study the *Chandas* and the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* hymns. [He recites: for the Ṛgveda, "I praise Agni, the domestic priest" (*agnim īḷe purohitam*); for the Yajurveda, "For sap, for strength" (*iṣe tvorje tvā*); for the Sāmaveda, "O Agni, come hither for our feast" (*agna āyāhi vītaye*); for the Atharvaveda, "May the divine waters be for our aid" (*śanno devīrabhiṣṭaye*). For the *Chandas*: "Agni is the head"; for the *Kūṣmāṇḍyas*: "Whatever offense we have committed against the gods. Whatever he studies, that [is his merit].

The *brahmayajña* is that which one offers as a recitation; the *devayajña* is that which one offers as an oblation; the *pitṛyajña* is that which one offers as the *svadhā* to the ancestors; the *bhūtayajña* is that which one brings as a Bali offering to the elemental beings; and the *manuṣyayajña* is that which one gives as food to guests—these indeed are the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*). When these are constantly and properly performed, they lead one to the supreme goal. For him from whom even one of these five sacrifices is omitted, an oblation with the *manasvatī* verse is prescribed as an expiation.

If [the rites] have been omitted through negligence for two or three days, one should offer three *tantumatī* oblations and recite four *vāruṇī* verses; if they have been interrupted for ten or twelve days, however, one must in all cases offer four *abhyāvartinī* oblations and perform the *tāntumata* rice-porridge sacrifice. If a woman or an unmarried man brings these offerings in his house, the *kūśmāṇḍī* verses should be offered there; having offered them for the prosperity of the sacrifice, [one should proceed].
When one goes on a journey and there is no one in his house to perform these five great duties, he departs accompanied by those sacrifices; and while away,
he performs them with whatever food is available.
If food is not produced, one should conclude these [rites] with water alone; having performed the vow with water itself and following it according to what is obtained,
the twice-born reach identity of nature with the gods through the sacrifice to the gods.
By the sacrifice to the ancestors one attains identity with the ancestors; by the sacrifice to the elemental spirits, with the elemental spirits;
by the sacrifice to men, with Manu; and by the sacrifice to Brahman, with Brahman.
Having attained identity with these, one dwells for a hundred years among the deities.

"They go to the blissful Brahman, which is firm, eternal, and imperishable. (15) Regarding the *nāndī-śrāddha*: on the day before [the festival], or according to the instruction, one should feed an even number of Brāhmaṇas during the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*). The ritual procedure (*upacāra*) is performed from left to right (*pradakṣiṇa*): having kindled the fire, having strewn *dūrvā* grass around it, having placed purifiers (*pavitra*) at the places of eating, and having set them down in the vessels; having purified [the water] and placed barley grains therein, the ritual procedure is carried out as for the *praṇītā* water. Having set out sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), and curd-rice (*dadhyodana*), the reception of the water and the dismissal are performed with the formula, "May the *nāndīmukha* ancestors be pleased," and likewise for the Viśvedevas.

Having offered with the mantra, "Svāhā to the Nāndīmukha ancestors," he spreads an underlayer of ghee, cuts off portions of all the food twice each, sprinkles them with ghee, and touches them while reciting a verse addressed to Viṣṇu. After they have sipped water, he gives the full vessel (pūrṇapātra). Having smeared the ground with cow-dung and sprinkled the remains of the curd-rice with barley-water, he places it down. Then follows the final sprinkling of water. Having asked, "Is it completed? he should mutter the remainder of the Anuvāka beginning with "The Iḍā is the invoker of the gods. After feeding the Brahmins, he causes them to pronounce blessings. 16.

The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is performed after one year, or in the eleventh month, the sixth, the fourth, or on the twelfth day; if an auspicious time (*puṇyāha*) should arrive, he should perform the invocation of the ancestors (*pitṛ-āvāhana*). Having touched the earth with the thumb and the ring finger of his left hand, he should recite: "Those ancestors who are on earth, those in the intermediate space, those in heaven, and those who have become immortal."

With the mantra, "May they, being immortal, rejoice in this sacrifice," he fills four vessels with sesame seeds, fragrant water, and milk—one for the deceased (preta) and three for the ancestors (pitṛs), or one vessel for the ancestors and pours it into the vessels of the ancestors while reciting the two verses beginning with "ye samānā ye sajātā. He says, "This is thy sesame-water together with the fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers; for thee, Svadhā! Homage! Thus is the offering of sesame-water. One should adapt the procedures for the offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*) and the assignment of portions (*anudeśanīya*) according to the purpose. In the *sapiṇḍī* rite, the pouring [of the water] is performed in this manner.
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is explained according to one's faith; from this point forward, it is performed with the monthly śrāddha. 17.

Now we shall describe those expiations for domestic rites (*gṛhya-prāyaścitta*) that are recorded in tradition; the remaining ones shall pertain to the sacrificial fires (*vaitānika*), because of the traditional enumeration of the deities of the oblations and because of the mention of their fruits. "Whatever deities belong to the *agnihotra*, they belong to the *aupāsana* fire; whatever is the duty of one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), that same is the duty of the one who maintains the *aupāsana* fire; whatever world belongs to the one who has established the sacred fires, that same world belongs to the one who maintains the *aupāsana* fire"—so says the *Śāṭyāyani-Brāhmaṇa*. In that [sacrificial context], those which are *puroḍāśas* (cake-offerings) here become *carus* (boiled offerings); the preparation of milk, curds, and speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) is like that of clarified butter (*ājya*); there is no placing of the curds over the fire.

When [the oblation] is near [to being spoiled], one should perform a sprinkling with water; and having performed the rites of the Raudra, Rākṣasa, Nairṛta, and Paitṛka [offerings], as well as cutting, piercing, digging, casting out, smelling, and touching oneself, one should touch water. In every case where [the oblation] has been spilled, broken, dried up, burnt, inverted, or obstructed, one offers two *mindā* oblations with the two verses: "Whatever deficiency has occurred in my self" (*yan ma ātmano mindābhūt*) and "Agni has given back my sight" (*punar agniś cakṣur adāt*). Then, regarding what has been spilled, one consecrates it with the verse "I sprinkle thee" (*saṃ tvā siñcāmi*), pours water over it with the verse "Make the earth swell" (*unnambhaya pṛthivīm*), and [proceeds].

Having worshipped with "Bhūḥ," he offers an oblation with the words, "The sky has stepped upon the earth. Now, if it is clarified butter, the consecration formula is, "O gods, you have come to the sacrifice. He should give something as a gift. If [the vessel] is broken, he consecrates the broken piece with, "The earth has gone to the earth," pours water over it with, "Undeflected, protect the earth," and should offer it into the fire with the verse, "Thirty-three are the threads... If it is made of wood, he throws it into the fire. Then, if it is scorched, he consecrates the burnt piece with, "To Nirṛti, thee! and [recites], "Thou art turned away, thou art turned downward; thou art the Rākṣasas..."

Saying "Go! toward the south-west or the north-west direction, he casts [the fire] toward that; then he should offer three oblations of clarified butter with the mantra, "The fires drive away the Rakṣasas. (18)

If another [offering] that is not fit for sacrifice arrives as a portion of this [oblation], one should set it aside, perform this [rite] with it, and offer it with this [formula]. By this, the cases of the undercooked (*aśṛta*) and the badly cooked (*duḥśṛta*) are explained. One should throw it into water; wherever one places fuel on the fire, it is known that one does so with the utterance of *svāhā*. Having consecrated the undercooked with "To Rudra, thee! and the badly cooked with "To Yama, thee!", then, in the event of the burning of the surrounding grass (*paristaraṇa*), [one should offer]: "Homage to Agni Kṣāmavat! Homage! O Kṣāmavat, do not harm me; do not harm my house, my wealth, my offspring, nor my..."

Having consecrated the animals with the mantra "paśūn," he should offer an oblation with the words, "Obeisance, obeisance to Agni Kṣāmavat. Then, having strewn the grass around again with the mantra "indraṃ vo viśvataḥ pari," he should offer an oblation with "indrāya svāhā. Now, regarding the burning of the enclosing sticks: he should offer [the burnt stick] with "obeisance, obeisance to the forest-fire Agni" (pradāvyāyāgnaye namo namaḥ pradāvyāya). From this point onward, the procedure is the same. He should offer an oblation with "thou art the fuel of Agni" for the western half, "thou art the fuel of Yama" for the southern half, and "thou art the fuel of Soma" for the northern half. With the mantra "kindling thee for a hundred winters," he should offer an oblation; if it is spoiled, he should offer another.

He should place [the fire] with the mantras "Thou art a Gandharva," and so on for each mantra. Now, in case of an omission, he should offer four oblations with the mantras "Thou, O Agni, art ours," "So thou, O Agni, art ours," "O Agni, thou art the leader," and "O Prajāpati"; and he should perform these same [mantras] when [the fire] has been omitted, adding the fifth mantra "May the mind, the light, enjoy [the offering]" as the fifth. And if he should realize this only after the rite is completed, he should give some gift. 19.

When the subsequent time arrives, the *homa* of the preceding [time] has ceased; this is what is meant by "transgression of time" (*kālātipatti*). For that, the expiation is as follows: having offered the oblation for the former with the mantra "The mind is the light" (*mano jyotiḥ*), one should offer the oblation for the latter. In this manner, one should perform the compensatory oblations (*pratihoma*) until ten nights have passed. Beyond that, up to twenty nights, there should be breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). Up to thirty nights, there should be fasting (*upavāsa*). Beyond that, up to sixty nights, one should fast for three nights. Beyond that, the *Prājāpatya* penance is prescribed. From the eleventh day onwards, one should also recite the *Tantumati* verses three times: "O Thread... (*tantum...*).

"Spreading [the sacrifice], awaken, O Agni; thirty-three are the threads"—having said this, or even "O Agni, you are the wind," he should offer oblations. From one night up to three nights, [he recites] "The mind is light"; from there upwards up to seven nights, and from there upwards up to twelve nights, he should fast for three nights. Beyond that, the Prājāpatya penance is prescribed. Starting from the eleventh day, the *tantumatī* verses are recited three times; it is stated that if the sacrifice has been interrupted for twelve days, the fasting begins from the eleventh day as before. 20.

Now, when a festival day (*parvan*) has passed, one should offer four oblations of clarified butter with the mantras "The mind is the light," "O Agni, go forth," "Whatever [sin] in this, O Agni," and "May Indra grant us well-being," and then prepare a cooked mess of grain (*sthālīpāka*). This should be done before the eighth day. Beyond that, one must observe a fast; for two [omissions], two [fasts] are required, and for three, three—thus it is in the case of occasional rites (*naimittika*) that have been neglected. When the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*) has been omitted, the expiation consists of an oblation as in the *pārvaṇa* rite. When the fortnightly period has passed, a fast must be observed; this is established as the rule for obligatory rites (*nitya*) as well. Now, regarding the Great Sacrifices (*mahāyajña*), [the expiation is] "The mind is the light."

Having offered three *tantumatī* oblations for two, three, four, or five [missed recitations]—starting from the sixth [day]—one should mutter the four *vāruṇī* verses: "imaṃ me varuṇa," "tattvā yāmi," "yacciddhi te," and "yatkiṃ ca. From the ninth night onwards, up until the tenth night, having offered four *abhyāvartinī* oblations, a *caru* sacrifice to Tanūnapāt must be performed. This applies even to a *snātaka* in the event of an interruption in the fire-oblation; when the *prājāpatya* penance is required, there is an interruption for him, and for him there is a re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*). [The verses are: "mano jyotiḥ," the *tantumatī*s, "punaḥ tvā," and the Āditya verses.

One should apply the *pūrṇāhuti* with the mantra "O Rudras" in all cases of injury to the fires; likewise for women during the *homa*, the approach to the wife (*abhigamana*), and the *sthālīpāka*. At the end of all these, one should use the *vyāhṛtis*. Thus it is established. Homage to the teachers, homage to the teachers. 21. Thus ends the third book in the *Bhāradvāja-sūtra*;
the *Gṛhyasūtra* of the Bhāradvāja school is completed.
